Projected Distillation: On Learning to Solve Hard Problems from Close, Correct Targets

Shripad V. Deshmukh2 Christian Bock1 Kangrui Ruan1 Abhijeet Awasthi1
Vijay Lingam1 Rein Houthooft1 Manish Prajapat1
1AWS AI Labs   2University of Massachusetts ††thanks: Work done during an internship at AWS AI Labs.††thanks: Corresponding author: manispj@amazon.com
Abstract

On-policy learning is central to post-training: training on a model’s own generations limits distribution shift and helps preserve existing capabilities. On hard problems, however, on-policy RL provides no reward-based learning signal when all attempts fail. On-policy distillation provides next-token supervision from a teacher, but on hard problems, if a rollout goes wrong early, subsequent supervision is conditioned on prefixes that already contain the mistake. Correct behavior can instead come from a gold or teacher solution, but such off-policy targets can differ substantially from the model’s generations and, as we show, may erode existing capabilities. We therefore treat on-policyness as a continuum and propose projected distillation, which minimally edits the student’s failed attempts into correct targets. The method uses contrastive updates to favor corrections over failed attempts and refreshes these corrections as the student evolves, enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail. Theoretically, we prove that the student’s learning regret grows with the edit size: it scales linearly with the horizon under minimal correction, as in DAgger, and quadratically under full-answer replacement, as in behavior cloning. Empirically, across two students (Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B) and five domains spanning math, code, science, and tool use, projected distillation gives the highest area under the specialization–retention frontier (best on 88 of 99 cells against GRPO and OPD, and 77 of 99 against SPOT and SODA). Our ablations highlight the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness: moving targets farther off-policy steadily worsens the specialization–retention trade-off, with retention falling from 0.9160.916 to 0.7440.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions.

†† Accepted at two NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Towards Test-Time Continual Learning Agents (TTCL) and Foundations of LLM Post-Training in Changing Environments (FLLMPT).

1 Introduction

Post-training adapts general-purpose language models to reason, follow instructions, and use tools. The dominant approaches are reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR; Shao et al., 2024; Schulman et al., 2017), distillation from a stronger teacher (Agarwal et al., 2023), and supervised fine-tuning (Wei et al., 2022). Across these approaches, the training signal is most effective when it remains on-policy, that is, close to the model’s own output distribution. Updates near this distribution can strengthen the target behavior while preserving capabilities acquired during pretraining (Agarwal et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). Post-training is particularly important for models with only a few billion parameters: although they are inexpensive to run and easy to deploy, they often lack the proficiency required for specialized tasks. We study how to teach such models to solve hard problems that they currently answer only rarely, if at all, without degrading their existing capabilities.

A fundamental challenge of on-policy RL is that on very hard problems the on-policy signal disappears. RLVR requires the model to succeed occasionally, so when every sampled attempt fails the reward is zero everywhere and nothing is reinforced. On-policy distillation (OPD; Agarwal et al., 2023) keeps the update on the model’s own rollouts and corrects them token by token to be closer to a response of a stronger teacher. However, the student rollout of a difficult task contains many mistakes: feedback on the later tokens is computed on top of an already-wrong prefix, so it largely patches earlier errors instead of teaching the step at hand (Zhang et al., 2026). Additionally, the later-token feedback in OPD is inefficient: as the student learns, the prefix on which later-token feedback was given and training budget was spent becomes less probable.

Alternatively, the training signal can come from a complete correct answer supplied from outside, either ground-truth data or a stronger teacher’s solution. Unlike OPD, which corrects the student’s own rollout token by token, this target replaces the rollout entirely: the whole training budget goes on producing a correct answer rather than on patching the one the student wrote. Such a target is drawn from a distribution other than the student’s own, so it is off-policy. The further it lies from what the student would produce, the more the student specializes on the task while eroding its abilities elsewhere. This suggests keeping the target a complete correct answer but choosing the one closest to what the student already writes, so the supervision stays near-on-policy.

Several recent works pursue similar ideas. SPOT (Lin and Han, 2026), SODA (Chen et al., 2026), and SuperCorrect (Yang et al., 2025) fix the student’s mistakes with a strong black-box teacher and learn from the corrections. What they leave unexamined is the on-policyness of the correction itself, how it changes with the size of the edit, and whether refreshing the corrections online against the evolving student matters. We focus on these aspects. We call the recipe of minimal, online corrections projected distillation (Fig. 1) and study it along five axes: how well it learns from close, correct solutions relative to other post-training approaches; why the edit must be minimal to keep the correction near-on-policy; why the corrections must be refreshed against the still-training student; which objective learns best from a correction; and how the projector itself can be improved. A regret analysis in the imitation-learning setting shows the importance of the edit size.

Our contributions.

  1. 1.

    We introduce projected distillation, a post-training recipe that learns from minimal, online corrections of the student’s mistakes. It needs only the correction text, so any capable black-box model can serve as the projector. Across two students and five benchmarks it attains the best specialization–retention trade-off, and retains prior abilities where standard post-training forgets on continual-learning metrics (Sec. 4.1).

  2. 2.

    Holding correctness fixed, we show that the correction must be both minimal and online. Pushing it off-policy monotonically worsens the trade-off (Sec. 4.2), and freezing the pool instead of refreshing it makes it collapse as the student drifts (Sec. 4.3). We further give an efficient training objective, a diff-localized contrast with self-training on correct rollouts (Sec. 4.4), and a refinement procedure that improves the projections from a mid-capacity (3232B) teacher without updating its parameters (Sec. 4.5).

  3. 3.

    We theoretically analyze projected distillation through imitation learning. The edit size interpolates between DAgger’s linear-in-horizon regret and behavior cloning’s quadratic regret (Sec. 5).

2 Related Work

Methods for improving a model on hard problems. Approaches differ in where the correct target comes from and how far that target lies from the model’s own distribution; together these largely determine the specialization–retention trade-off. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR; GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), PPO (Schulman et al., 2017)) draws the target from the model’s own rollouts, but on the pass​@​k=0\mathrm{pass}@k{=}0 set every rollout is wrong and no signal remains. On-policy distillation (GKD (Agarwal et al., 2023)) and self-distillation (Yang et al., 2024) keep the update on those rollouts while matching a teacher’s token distribution, which requires teacher logits. Supervised fine-tuning on an external gold or teacher solution supplies correctness directly but is maximally off-policy, so fitting it forgets. Between these, there is scope to manufacture a correct target based on the student’s attempt. This opens up the possibility of treating the correct solutions along a continuum from on-policy to off-policy with respect to the model’s current generation style. Our work studies how far the edits may go, whether they need to be recomputed as the model changes, and what objective to use for effective learning.

Closest work. The literature presents approaches similar to ours: LeMa (An et al., 2023) mines corrections once, from an assortment of models rather than the student, with free-form rewrites and an objective that uses response likelihood maximization. SPOT (Lin and Han, 2026) gathers mistakes of the base model, rectifies the mistakes using minimal edits from an oracle, creates a preference dataset and learns with a reward-based binary cross-entropy objective. SODA (Chen et al., 2026) creates mistake–correction pairs without emphasizing minimal edits, performs an SFT warm-up, and then, with the SFT’ed policy fixed, learns from static preference pairs. SuperCorrect (Yang et al., 2025) distills thought templates from a teacher and applies collaborative DPO over the teacher’s correction traces. We also work in the hard-task regime where the model fails. However, our paper focuses mainly on the regime of online learning from close, correct targets to teach the student how to effectively solve hard tasks. We perform a controlled study of the edit sizes used to provide corrections (Sec. 4.2), static vs. online-refreshed pools of corrections (Sec. 4.3) and effective learning objectives for black-box learning (Sec. 4.4). In addition, we theoretically analyze how the edit-size influences the learning regret, which distinguishes our work from the previous ones. Concurrent work (Karan et al., 2026) explores self-projection with an MCMC sampler, in which the student itself rewrites its response with the reference solution in view; Appendix I compares it with black-box projection on its math benchmark.

3 Projected Distillation

We study post-training on problems the model rarely solves, where its own samples earn no reward and correctness has to come from outside.

Setup. Given a problem xx, a solution is a token sequence y∈𝒱≤Hy\in\mathcal{V}^{\leq H} drawn from a vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V} with a generation horizon HH. The student produces yy autoregressively via πθS​(y∣x)=∏tπθS​(yt∣x,y<t)\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y\mid x)=\prod_{t}\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}), where yty_{t} denotes the tt-th token, y<ty_{<t} its prefix, and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} the frozen initialization of the student. Correctness is judged by a verifier R⁡(x,y)∈{0,1}R(x,y)\in\{0,1\} (e.g., exact-match checking or unit tests), inducing the set of accepted solutions 𝒞⁡(x)={y:R⁡(x,y)=1}\mathcal{C}(x)=\{y:R(x,y)=1\}. Our focus is on problems that lie beyond the student’s current ability, i.e., pass​@​k=0\mathrm{pass}@k{=}0 set, for which all kk sampled attempts fail. Further, in Sec. 5, we formalize the generation process using a dynamic-token sequence MDP to provide theoretical insights.

Projection. The accepted set 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x) typically contains many solutions, but these solutions can differ substantially in likelihood under the student. Training toward a solution the student already considers likely requires less movement of its output distribution and therefore better preserves unrelated capabilities (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2022). We therefore choose, among the verifier-accepted solutions in 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x), the one with highest likelihood under the student.

Definition 1 (Projection).

For a student πθS\pi_{\theta_{S}} and a problem xx, the projection is the correct answer the student is most likely to produce, proj⁡(x)∈arg​maxy′∈𝒞⁡(x)​log​πθS​(y′∣x)\mathrm{proj}(x)\in\argmax_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}(x)}\log\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y^{\prime}\mid x).

Practically, searching the true projection within 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x) is intractable. We propose to find a close approximation with the help of the student’s attempt itself. The intuition behind this is that a wrong attempt is a sample from the student and is therefore already likely under it; a correction that preserves most of its tokens preserves most of that likelihood, while the verifier places the result in 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x). Minimal editing is thus a tractable surrogate for Definition 1, with the verifier supplying correctness and the retained tokens supplying proximity. We test the surrogate directly in Sec. 4.2, varying the edit size and recording the likelihood shift Λ=log⁡πθS​(y+∣x)−log⁡πθS​(y−∣x)\Lambda=\log\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y^{+}\mid x)-\log\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y^{-}\mid x) that each size demands. A projector receives the problem and the attempt in context and is prompted to make the smallest change that corrects the answer (examples in Appendix B; prompts in Sec. C.3).

Learning from projection. In each round we prompt the student on the hard problems and collect a batch of responses. Most of them are wrong. We write y−y^{-} for a wrong response and y+y^{+} for its projection, and ycy^{\mathrm{c}} for the responses the student gets correct on its own. We have access only to the text the projector returns, not to its logits, so we cannot match its token distribution. We learn from the pair (y−,y+)(y^{-},y^{+}) by preference instead. The projection edits only a small part of the attempt, so y−y^{-} and y+y^{+} agree almost everywhere, and a contrast over their full length would spend most of its gradient on text that was already correct. We therefore restrict the contrast to the tokens the edit changed. A token-diff of y−y^{-} against y+y^{+} marks a mistake span E−E^{-} and a fix span E+E^{+}; for instance, for y−=𝙰𝙱𝙲𝙳y^{-}=\mathtt{ABCD} and y+=𝙰𝚇𝙲𝚉y^{+}=\mathtt{AXCZ}, E−={𝙱,𝙳}E^{-}=\{\mathtt{B},\mathtt{D}\} and E+={𝚇,𝚉}E^{+}=\{\mathtt{X},\mathtt{Z}\}. We apply a DPO contrast (Rafailov et al., 2023) to those spans alone, using the frozen initialization πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} as reference and β\beta for its strength:

ℒDiff​-​Local​-​DPO=−𝔼x​log⁡σ⁡(β⁡[∑t∈E+log⁡πθS​(yt+∣x,y<t+)πref​(yt+∣x,y<t+)−∑t∈E−log⁡πθS​(yt−∣x,y<t−)πref​(yt−∣x,y<t−)]),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Diff\text{-}Local\text{-}DPO}}=-\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\,\log\sigma\!\Big(\beta\big[\textstyle\sum_{t\in E^{+}}\log\tfrac{\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y^{+}_{t}\mid x,\,y^{+}_{<t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^{+}_{t}\mid x,\,y^{+}_{<t})}-\sum_{t\in E^{-}}\log\tfrac{\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y^{-}_{t}\mid x,\,y^{-}_{<t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^{-}_{t}\mid x,\,y^{-}_{<t})}\big]\Big), (1)

Here σ\sigma is the logistic function. The contrast constrains only how likely y+y^{+} is relative to y−y^{-}, so we add a term that supervises the student’s own correct responses directly:

ℒProjected​-​Distillation=ℒDiff​-​Local​-​DPO+ℒSFT,whereℒSFT=−𝔼x∑tlogπθS(ytc∣x,y<tc).\!\!\!\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Projected\text{-}Distillation}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Diff\text{-}Local\text{-}DPO}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}},~\text{where}~~\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\,\textstyle\sum_{t}\log\pi_{\theta_{S}}(y^{\mathrm{c}}_{t}\mid x,y^{\mathrm{c}}_{<t}).\! (2)

Therefore, the wrong responses supply the contrast and the correct ones the supervised term. The next round re-prompts the student on the same problems and projects whatever it gets wrong then, so the targets follow the current policy. Fig. 2 summarizes one round of our approach. Sec. 4.3 compares rebuilding the targets each round against reusing a static correction pool, and Sec. 4.4 compares our loss (2) against five alternatives on the same data.

4 Experiments

First, we compare projected distillation with standard post-training approaches in the hard-task regime, and ask whether what a student learns on one benchmark’s hard set carries over to the hard problems of other benchmarks (Sec. 4.1). The remaining sections examine the recipe itself, each component of which could have been set differently: the correction may change more or fewer of the attempt’s tokens (Sec. 4.2), it may be computed once or recomputed as the student learns (Sec. 4.3), and several objectives may be applied to it (Sec. 4.4). We vary each in turn while holding the remainder fixed, then ask whether the projections can be improved further by test-time scaling (Sec. 4.5), and finally whether the same model can serve as its own projector when given privileged information (Sec. 4.6).

Experimental Setup: We study two instruction-tuned students from different families, Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025) and OLMo-2-7B (OLMo Team, 2024), on five benchmarks spanning math, code, tools and science: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2024), SciKnowEval (Feng et al., 2024), and ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023). For each (student, benchmark) pair we train only on its hard set: the problems on which the base student fails all k=16k{=}16 sampled attempts at temperature 0.80.8. The hard set is mined from the benchmark’s training split (Sec. C.2), and retention is measured in-domain on a disjoint held-out slice of the same benchmark. All methods use matched budgets for optimization updates and per-step generation. The remaining configuration is in Sec. C.1, with prompt templates in Sec. C.3 and further training details in Sec. C.4. Unless noted, results are averaged over 33 training seeds, and Sec. C.5 separates training-seed from evaluation-seed spread. Sec. D.3 additionally evaluates the trained checkpoints on suites they never saw, and Sec. D.5 on the hard problems of benchmarks they never saw.

Baselines. We compare against four baselines, each probing a different axis of the post-training design space. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) performs on-policy RL with verifiable rewards, where positive rewards are scarce. OPD (Agarwal et al., 2023) performs white-box distillation from the token-level logits of a strong teacher conditioned on the student’s own prefixes, using a same-family 32B teacher (Qwen3-32B or OLMo-2-32B) for each student; our method uses these same 32B teachers as its projection models, and both methods are given the gold answer as privileged information. Surgical Post-Training (SPOT; Lin and Han, 2026) minimally corrects the student’s initial attempts and trains on the resulting frozen preference data, while Semi-On-policy Distillation (SODA; Chen et al., 2026) fine-tunes the student on teacher corrections and then contrasts a teacher response against a frozen copy of that fine-tuned student. Against SPOT and SODA every method draws its corrections from one shared black-box model, which isolates the learning algorithm from the projector.

Metrics. We report specialization, pass@1 on the hard set, and retention, pass@1 on the held-out slice. A method can raise either at the other’s expense, so neither effectively ranks methods on its own. Our headline metric is the area under the specialization–retention Pareto frontier (AUPF), the retention a method sustains as it specializes further, anchored at a shared untrained base. AUPF is low both for a method that never specializes and for one that specializes by giving up retention. We report it alongside three continual-learning summaries of the retention trajectory, backward transfer (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017), forgetting (Chaudhry et al., 2018) and training-averaged accuracy (Kemker et al., 2018), and retention-safe specialization, the highest specialization reached while retention stays within ε\varepsilon of base. Full definitions are in Appendix D.

4.1 RQ1: How does projected distillation compare with baselines?

We compare against the four baselines, drawing our corrections first from a same-family 3232B teacher and then from a shared black-box projector, and report AUPF in Tab. 1, the continual-learning metrics in Tab. 3, and the pooled frontiers in Fig. 3.

Projected distillation attains the highest AUPF on eight of nine cells against GRPO and OPD and on seven of nine against SPOT and SODA (Tab. 1), under both projector settings. The margins are largest on SciKnowEval and ToolAlpaca, reaching 0.1790.179 against OPD’s 0.0270.027 on Qwen SciKnowEval and 0.6760.676 against 0.1280.128 on Qwen ToolAlpaca. The baselines are not short of specialization; SPOT and SODA both reach real hard-set accuracy (Tab. 3). However, they retain poorly. In Fig. 3 our frontier runs flat along the untrained base across the whole specialization range while every baseline’s falls away from it. Pooled across projectors, our mean AUPF is 0.2560.256 with the mid-capacity same-family 3232B teacher and 0.2750.275 with the black-box projector, so the mid-capacity projector performs slightly worse. In Sec. 4.5, we investigate how to improve learning with such a teacher.

The two baseline families fall short for different reasons. GRPO has little to learn from, since the hard set is mined at pass​@​k=0\mathrm{pass}@k{=}0; continued sampling still recovers occasional correct rollouts, enough for the highest specialization of any method on OLMo SciKnowEval, but its retention is the lowest there as well (Tab. 8), because reinforcing a rare correct rollout sharpens the student onto that solution at the expense of what it produces elsewhere (Yue et al., 2025). SPOT and SODA hold correct targets throughout, so they are not limited by correctness. They are rather limited by how far the correction moves the attempt and how often it is rebuilt, as shown further in sections 4.2 and 4.3. Three AUPF result cells are not in our favour. On Qwen MATH, SPOT and SODA fit the hard-set answers more closely, SODA reaching 0.1360.136 specialization against our 0.0310.031, and give up some retention for it (0.6640.664 against our 0.7600.760; Tab. 8). On Qwen SciKnowEval SODA leads on both axes, in the one cell whose retention carries a standard error of 0.1310.131 across seeds, several times that of any other method there. On OLMo GSM8K, OPD reaches 0.4960.496 specialization against our 0.2360.236 at comparable retention, so token-level feedback apparently keeps its effectiveness there.

Training on a hard set risks catastrophic forgetting due to limited model capacity, so Tab. 3 reports four continual-learning measures, each summarizing a whole run. Training-averaged specialization and retention give the mean of each axis over the run: ours is highest on specialization (x¯=0.264\bar{x}=0.264 and 0.2760.276 against SODA’s 0.2240.224) and holds retention at base (y¯norm=1.000\bar{y}_{\mathrm{norm}}=1.000 and 0.9950.995 against 0.7760.776), so what it gains is not paid for out of retention during training. Backward transfer is the net change in retention from the untrained base to the final checkpoint, and ours are the only values that are not significantly negative (0.0090.009 and −0.004-0.004). Forgetting is the drop from a run’s highest retention to its final retention, so it registers ability lost during training even when the endpoint looks acceptable: ours are 0.0840.084 and 0.1070.107 against 0.5090.509 for SPOT and 0.3550.355 for SODA, which specialize early and lose retention through the rest of training (Fig. 10). Retention-safe specialization, the most a run reaches at any checkpoint whose retention is within ε\varepsilon of base, is highest for both our variants at either tolerance. Retention here is measured on a held-out slice of the trained benchmark; Sec. D.3 evaluates the math-trained checkpoints on suites they never saw.

Transfer to other benchmarks’ hard problems. We test whether performance improvement on one benchmark’s hard problems extends to hard problems from other benchmarks. For this experiment, we train Qwen3-8B with each black-box method and with GRPO on 501501 MATH problems that it fails on all 1616 attempts. We evaluate it on 127127 held-out hard MATH problems not seen during training, and on 2,8852{,}885 hard problems from OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), Omni-MATH (Gao et al., 2024a), AIME 1983–2023 and DAPO-Math (Yu et al., 2025). More details of the setup are provided in Sec. D.5.

We report the results in Tab. 2. Projected distillation shows stronger performance than the baselines in hard-to-hard generalization. On the held-out MATH problems it raises pass@1 from 0.0130.013 to 0.0560.056 and pass@16 from 0.1500.150 to 0.3540.354, against 0.0310.031 and 0.2910.291 for the best baseline. On the four other benchmarks it raises pass@1 from 0.0110.011 to 0.0200.020 (+0.009±0.001+0.009\pm 0.001) and pass@16 from 0.1140.114 to 0.1540.154, where the best baseline gains 0.0050.005 in pass@1 and SPOT and GRPO gain nothing.

What the student learns on one benchmark’s hard problems therefore carries to hard problems it never trained on. In Sec. D.5, we provide a breakdown of the gain across individual benchmarks and an analysis of a projected distillation model trained on Omni-MATH.

4.2 RQ2: How does edit size influence learning in projected distillation?

A correction may be correct and still lie far from what the student would have produced, and this question concerns the cost of that distance. We construct four arms that hold correctness fixed and vary only how much the correction rewrites the attempt: a minimal edit, two progressively larger rewrites obtained by re-prompting the projector, and gold, the dataset’s GSM8K reference solution, which discards the attempt altogether. Each arm trains a separate Qwen3-8B student from the same base under identical hyperparameters, so only the target y+y^{+} varies; the rejected side remains the student’s own wrong rollout y−y^{-}. The projector rather than the prompt settles how much text is replaced, so we identify the arms by the edit size they realize and measure the distance a correction imposes by the likelihood shift it demands, Λ=log⁡πθ​(y+∣x)−log⁡πθ​(y−∣x)\Lambda=\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{+}\mid x)-\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{-}\mid x), reported as |Λ||\Lambda|.

Fig. 4 shows that among the three arms that differ only in edit size, relative specialization falls to 0.540.54 and then 0.450.45 of the minimal-edit arm and retention from 0.9160.916 to 0.8070.807, while Λ\Lambda falls from −86-86 to −433-433. The arms are equally correct, so what the larger rewrites cost is distance from the student. Gold sits outside that ordering: its edit is 926926 tokens, between the two rewrites, yet it specializes better than either (0.870.87 of the minimal edit) and returns the lowest retention of any arm (0.7440.744). The token count understates its distance, since gold keeps none of the attempt and counts small only because a reference solution is short; its likelihood shift does not say the same: at Λ=+3969\Lambda=+3969 it is the one arm the student finds more likely than its own attempt, the sign opposite to every rewrite, and that value is dominated by the length difference rather than lying on the rewrites’ scale. We therefore read edit size as the quantity governing the trade-off among matched rewrites, with the minimal edit best balanced, and report gold on the behavioral axes only; Appendix E gives the per-arm values and the mechanism measurements.

4.3 RQ3: How much does refreshing corrections online help?

Projected distillation recomputes its corrections at every round, so that each target is an edit of an attempt the current student has just produced. Naturally, we ask what role this mechanism plays in projected distillation learning. For comparison, we gather a static pool: minimal-edit corrections of the initial checkpoint’s responses, mined once before training and reused for the remainder of the run. This is the same regime occupied by methods like SPOT (Lin and Han, 2026) and LeMa (An et al., 2023). The projector for both static and online-refreshed arms is the same black-box projector. We report results pooled over all model×\timesbenchmark cells and three seeds in figure 5.

Refreshing the corrections is essential. Online refresh improves specialization steadily throughout training, reaching 0.370.37 pass@1, whereas the static pool rises over the first few updates and then flattens near 0.200.20 (Fig. 5, left). Retention separates more sharply: online refresh holds it at base for the whole run, while the static pool climbs slightly above base over the first 2525 steps, falls to 0.760.76 by step 5050, and declines from there to 0.600.60 (Fig. 5, right). The fall sets in once the pool has been reused for several rounds. A static pool cannot follow the student to the failures it develops afterwards, so repeated passes fit it to a fixed set of targets, while its generalization degrades.

4.4 RQ4: How best to learn from projections of wrong responses?

In a typical round of projected distillation, we have access to wrong attempts y−y^{-}, their corrections y+y^{+} and correct student responses ycy^{\mathrm{c}}. These three quantities admit several learning objectives, and in this section we study an effective objective for learning. The simplest is supervised fine-tuning on the projection, optionally combined with a term on the student’s own correct responses. Keeping only that second term is rejection fine-tuning (RFT; Yuan et al., 2023), which learns from the student’s successes alone and ignores the projection. Further, because the wrong attempt is also retained, a contrastive objective is available: DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) over the full response, again optionally combined with the self-SFT term. Since a minimal edit leaves most of the response unchanged, the contrast may instead be localized to the edited spans ((1)). We compare the six resulting recipes on the GSM8K hard set and report the outcome in Fig. 6.

The projection is necessary: training on the student’s own correct responses alone recovers 0.160.16 of the adopted recipe, since the hard set is mined at pass​@​k=0\mathrm{pass}@k{=}0 and the student’s rollouts stay correct on about 6%6\% of attempts through the run, so RFT has almost nothing to train on. Among objectives that do use the projection, the contrast is the more reliable choice: SFT on the projection reaches 0.810.81 on average but carries a standard error of 0.0780.078 across seeds, three to sixteen times that of any contrastive arm. The self-SFT term then settles the ordering among those arms. A contrast constrains the likelihood of y+y^{+} only relative to y−y^{-}, and a localized one does so over a handful of tokens, so both gain from a term that raises the likelihood of correct text outright, and the localized one gains more: without it the diff-localized contrast underperforms the full-sequence one (0.730.73 against 0.780.78), and with it the ordering reverses (1.001.00 against 0.920.92). We adopt the diff-localized contrast with self-SFT as the default recipe (Sec. 3); per-arm objectives and absolute values are in Appendix F.

4.5 RQ5: Can we improve the quality of projections for better learning?

In this section, we explore ways to make projections from a mid-capacity projector more effective. The natural approach would be to fine-tune the projector; we instead take a computationally efficient test-time route and ask a frozen Qwen3-32B to refine its own correction over several rounds. At each round it is re-prompted with its previous correction and the spans it edited, and across rounds we retain the valid correction most likely under the base student, measured by log-likelihood over the edited tokens. We sweep the refinement budget over K∈{0,1,2}K\in\{0,1,2\} on a Qwen3-8B student and the GSM8K hard set with the default recipe.

Refinement improves the corrections in two ways (Fig. 7). More of the student’s failures become correctable, the correction rate rising from 9.2%9.2\% at K=0K{=}0 to 15.4%15.4\% at K=1K{=}1 and 16.7%16.7\% at K=2K{=}2 (Fig. 7, left), so a larger part of the hard set contributes a training pair at all. At the same time the edits become smaller, from 256256 to 130130 tokens (Fig. 7, right), which by the account of Sec. 4.2 should make each target easier to learn from. Downstream, hard-set pass@1 rises from 0.370.37 to 0.440.44 while retention stays near 0.910.91–0.930.93, with most of the gain arriving in the first round. Test-time refinement can therefore improve the projections, leading to effective performance. Additional details are in Appendix G.

4.6 RQ6: Can we use the same model for projection given privileged information?

Use of the same model to provide the learning signal is a popular choice in post-training. One well-known example is on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026). Similarly, in this section, we test how much we can gain by replacing external projections with the model’s own self-projections given the ground truth answer. We experiment with Qwen3-8B on the GSM8K dataset. The full setup is provided in Appendix H.

Tab. 4 reports the result. Self-projection does produce usable corrections: the student lifts its hard set from 0.0000.000 to 0.2190.219 while retention stays at 0.9240.924, so a model that is told the answer can repair enough of its own reasoning to learn from it. It does not, however, substitute for a stronger projector. The black-box projector reaches 0.5600.560 on the same problems, and even the student-agnostic gold solution reaches 0.4890.489. Concurrent work (Karan et al., 2026) proposes a self-projection scheme of its own, in which an MCMC sampler has the student rewrite its response with a reference solution in view, and Appendix I compares it against black-box projection on its own math benchmark.

5 A Patch-MDP Analysis of Projected Distillation

Setup. We model generation as a deterministic patch MDP with a token budget HH (Definition 2). A state is a prompt together with the tokens generated so far. An action is a patch, a span of tokens appended to that state, and every token carries a reward in [0,1][0,1]. A patch may span several tokens, but the reward and every bound below decompose token by token (Lemma 1), so decisions are indexed by token position throughout and HH counts them. The student is a policy π\pi in a class Π\Pi, with expected return J⁡(π)J(\pi) and optimum J⋆J^{\star}. Choosing action ww at state ss forfeits some return against the best action available in ss. We denote this optimality gap with Δ⁡(s,w)\Delta(s,w), which is upper-bounded by a constant Δmax\Delta_{\max} (Definition 3). Owing to telescoping (Lemma 1), a full rollout’s shortfall can be accounted for one token at a time. The regret J⋆−J⁡(π)J^{\star}-J(\pi) then equals HH times the average per-token optimality gap, taken over π\pi’s state occupancy (Lemma 2). We write mm for the edit size (Definition 4): the tokens the correction changes relative to the attempt, counted over the HH decisions Definition 2 gives both and so including the padding that equalizes their lengths. It relates to the token diff |E+|+|E−||E^{+}|+|E^{-}| of Sec. 3, the quantity Sec. 4.2 reports, by m=|E+|+|E−|+||E+|−|E−||=2​max⁡(|E+|,|E−|)m=|E^{+}|+|E^{-}|+\big||E^{+}|-|E^{-}|\big|=2\max(|E^{+}|,|E^{-}|), the extra term being the change in answer length. Secs. J.1 and J.2 give the full treatment.
Learning protocol. Training runs for MM rounds. Each round is one batch of rollouts, the corrections made to them, and the gradient update that follows. πi\pi_{i} is the policy entering round ii. Ideally we would query the projector at every student mistake as the student generates a response. That would let us minimize the gap under the student’s own state occupancy. This is exactly the DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) approach, where an expert labels states under the learner’s own occupancy, leading to a learning regret of O⁡(H)O(H), linear in the horizon. Per-mistake labeling as an LLM student responds is infeasible, since it demands a projector call and a forward pass at every mistake. In projected distillation, we instead correct the rollout once and perform a single forward pass over the response. This minimizes the optimality gap under a state occupancy drifted away from the student’s own.
Fitting error. The projector edits the student’s wrong response such that for each state in the rewritten response, the next token has zero optimality gap. We define two further quantities: (i) the policy fit error ε~\tilde{\varepsilon}, the irreducible error in fitting the best policy in the class to the expert projections; and (ii) the optimization term γ~M\tilde{\gamma}_{M}, the student’s excess disagreement over that best policy, which vanishes for a no-regret learner (Definition 5). Since a single disagreement costs at most Δmax\Delta_{\max}, the gap loss at these prefixes is bounded by Δmax\Delta_{\max} times the disagreement rate (Lemma 3).
We assume that the drift caused by earlier token edits at a given decision point has a smooth, bounded effect on the optimality gap. We denote the maximum per-token effect on the optimality gap by η\eta.

Assumption 1 (Prefix sensitivity).

Write e⁡(s,s′)e(s,s^{\prime}) for the number of insertions and deletions carrying the generated tokens of one history into those of the other (Definition 4). The map s↦𝔼w∼π(⋅∣s)[Δ(s,w)]s\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)}[\Delta(s,w)] is η\eta-Lipschitz in that count:

|𝔼w∼π(⋅∣s′)[Δ(s′,w)]−𝔼w∼π(⋅∣s)[Δ(s,w)]|≤ηe(s,s′)∀π∈Π,∀s,s′.\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s^{\prime})}[\Delta(s^{\prime},w)]-\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)}[\Delta(s,w)]\bigr|\;\leq\;\eta\,e(s,s^{\prime})\qquad\forall\,\pi\in\Pi,\ \forall\,s,s^{\prime}.
Theorem 1 (Best-iterate suboptimality of projected distillation).

Let Assumption 1 hold, let the projector be as above, and let mm be the mean edit size over the rounds. Then after MM rounds

mini≤M⁡[J⋆−J⁡(πi)]≤H​Δmax​(ε~+γ~M)+η​m​H.\min_{i\leq M}\big[J^{\star}-J(\pi_{i})\big]\;\leq\;H\,\Delta_{\max}\,\big(\tilde{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}_{M}\big)\;+\;\eta\,m\,H.

The first term collects the fitting and optimization costs. The second is drift, which does not decrease with MM; a smaller edit is the only lever on it.
Horizon regimes. For a minimal edit the edit size is m=O⁡(1)m=O(1), making the drift O⁡(η​H)O(\eta H) and hence the regret O⁡(H)O(H), linear in the horizon. A complete rewrite of the response leads to m=Θ⁡(H)m=\Theta(H), making the drift O⁡(η​H2)O(\eta H^{2}) and therefore the regret O⁡(H2)O(H^{2}), quadratic in the horizon (Corollary 1). In a controlled experiment in Sec. 4.2 we vary mm (Definition 4) and observe that the student’s performance suffers as the edit size increases. The two endpoints recover the rates of DAgger and of behavior cloning, though not those algorithms themselves.

6 Conclusion

We introduced projected distillation, a post-training recipe to enable lower-capacity LLMs to solve hard problems beyond their current reach. We demonstrated that standard on-policy post-training methods such as RLVR and OPD struggle to specialize on the hard task, while training on gold solutions leads to catastrophic forgetting. Our proposed approach avoids these issues by maintaining rich learning targets close to the student’s current policy. This is done by iteratively transforming the student’s failed attempts into correct solutions through minimal edits. Our extensive empirical analyses showed that our approach achieved a better specialization–retention Pareto frontier than previous approaches. We showed that it is important to learn from minimal edits rather than from larger edits or full rewrites, and from the mistakes of the latest checkpoint rather than only those of the base model. Theoretical analysis with a smoothness assumption on the effects of token edits described a spectrum where minimal edits lead to DAgger-like linear-in-horizon regret, while full rewrites lead to behavior-cloning-like quadratic regret. Thus, our work provides empirical and theoretical evidence on the utility of the underlying continuum of on-policyness for continual learning on hard tasks.

Limitations and future work. We instantiate the projection as a minimal token edit; exploring likelihood-based alternatives is also an important future direction. The uniform per-token sensitivity assumed in Assumption 1 may be strong and needs further investigation. Our recipe assumes a cheap correctness check, leaving open the domains without a readily available verifier. We also study single-turn tasks, where the student produces one response and the projector edits that response. Multi-turn tasks, in which a failure can originate several turns before it becomes visible in the outcome, would require deciding which turn to project, and we leave this to future work.
