Appendix B Projection examples

This appendix shows complete wrong→\toprojected pairs, so the minimal-edit property can be read at the level of full solutions. In each pair the projector reuses the student’s derivation verbatim and changes only what is needed to make the answer correct; the changed spans are the token-diff E−E^{-} (mistake) and E+E^{+} (fix) that the diff-local DPO loss (1) contrasts. All student answers are from Qwen3-8B (base); all projections are from the black-box projector. Sec. B.1 works through the single-edit example of Fig. 8 in full, and Sec. B.2 a multi-edit one.

B.1 A single edit: Cindy’s wishing pond

Problem. Cindy tosses 5 dimes into the wishing pond. Eric flips 3 quarters into the pond. Garrick throws in 8 nickels. Ivy then drops 60 pennies in. If Eric dips his hands into the water and pulls out a quarter, how much money, in cents, did they put into the pond? (Gold: 200.)

y−y^{-} (rejected, wrong — #### 225)
Dimes: 5×10=505\times 10=50. Quarters: 3×25=753\times 25=75. Nickels: 8×5=408\times 5=40. Pennies: 60×1=6060\times 1=60. Total =50+75+40+60=225=50+75+40+60=225. #### 225

y+y^{+} (chosen, minimal edit — #### 200)
Dimes: 5×10=505\times 10=50. Quarters: 3×25=753\times 25=75. Nickels: 8×5=408\times 5=40. Pennies: 60×1=6060\times 1=60. Total =50+75+40+60=225=50+75+40+60=225. Eric removes a quarter: 225−25=200225-25=200. #### 200

The entire count is reused verbatim; the projector inserts the single step the student omitted (subtracting the withdrawn quarter). The token-diff is a one-span edit: E−={#### 225}E^{-}=\{\texttt{\#\#\#\# 225}\}, E+={E^{+}=\{“Eric removes…=200=200”,#### 200},\texttt{\#\#\#\# 200}\}.

B.2 Several edits: John’s computer

Problem. John’s new computer cost $1500. He needs a monitor and other peripherals that cost 1/5 that much. He also wants to upgrade the $300 video card in the base computer with one that costs twice as much. How much did he spend? (Gold: 2100.)

y−y^{-} (rejected, wrong — #### 2400)
Computer: $1500. Peripherals: 15×1500=300\tfrac{1}{5}\times 1500=300. Upgraded video card: 2×300=6002\times 300=600. Total: 1500+300+600=24001500+300+600=2400. #### 2400

y+y^{+} (chosen, minimal edit — #### 2100)
Computer: $1500. Peripherals: 15×1500=300\tfrac{1}{5}\times 1500=300. Upgraded video card: 2×300=6002\times 300=600. Since the base computer already includes the $300 card, he pays only the extra: 600−300=300600-300=300. Total: 1500+300+300=21001500+300+{\color[rgb]{0.1055,0.4688,0.2148}\textbf{300}}=2100. #### 2100

Here two spans change—the video-card line and the total—while the computer and peripheral steps are reused unchanged. This is a multi-edit projection: the correction threads the fix (charging only the upgrade difference) through to the final sum.

Appendix C Experimental setup

C.1 Reproducibility Details

Model families and projectors. The two students are open-weight instruction-tuned models from different families, Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025) and OLMo-2-7B (OLMo Team, 2024), chosen so the effect is tested as a property of the method rather than of one pretraining recipe. The same-family projector shares the student’s tokenizer, as OPD requires, and unless noted it is Qwen3-32B for the Qwen student and OLMo-2-32B for the OLMo student. The black-box path (Sec. 3) needs only the correction text, so it is tokenizer-free and draws its corrections from a single black-box model shared across students. The exact checkpoints are: students Qwen/Qwen3-8B and allenai/OLMo-2-1124-7B-Instruct; same-family 3232B teachers Qwen/Qwen3-32B and allenai/OLMo-2-0325-32B-Instruct.

Benchmarks. Five benchmarks spanning math, code, tools, and science, each contributing a mined hard set for training and a held-out slice for evaluation:

  • •

    GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021): grade-school math, numeric answers graded by exact match. Mine from the 7,473-example train split; evaluate on a 200200-problem held-out slice of the test split.

  • •

    MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b): competition math, \boxed{} answers graded by symbolic equivalence. Mine from the 12k train split; evaluate on the MATH-500 slice (Lightman et al., 2023).

  • •

    ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023): tool use and API calling. Mine from the 468468-API, ∼4,255{\sim}4{,}255-instance release. The model must emit the first tool call for a request, and a call counts as correct when the action is a valid function of that API, its arguments parse as JSON with all required parameters present, and the action matches the reference call.

  • •

    LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2024): contamination-resistant competitive-programming problems, graded by unit-test execution (pass@1). Mine hard problems from the v6 release; evaluate on a held-out slice.

  • •

    SciKnowEval (Feng et al., 2024): multi-level scientific knowledge. We use the L3 four-choice subset (4,1354{,}135 items) of the 28,39228{,}392-item release, graded by a letter match against the reference option.

Evaluation protocol. Specialization and retention are evaluated identically at step 00 and every 2525 steps thereafter, so each student and benchmark serves as its own reference; the continual-learning summaries built from these two series are defined in Appendix D. Every benchmark is scored by the grader listed above, always as sampled pass@1 on its held-out slice, a 200200-problem slice for GSM8K. The full-suite evaluations of Sec. D.3 instead score the final checkpoints on complete test splits. Answer extraction is per benchmark: the ####-delimited final number for GSM8K, with a last-number fallback for free-form generations; the \boxed{} expression for MATH, compared by symbolic equivalence; the final Answer: letter for SciKnowEval; the first Action and Action Input pair for ToolAlpaca; and the extracted program for LiveCodeBench, executed against the unit tests.

Hardware and software. The main experiments ran on a single pod of 8×8\times NVIDIA A100-SXM4 (40 GB) GPUs, which was the compute available to us. The stack is PyTorch 2.8.0 (CUDA 12.8), TRL 1.6.0 (von Werra et al., 2020), Transformers 5.12.1, and Accelerate 1.14.0. Multi-GPU training uses fully-sharded data parallelism (FSDP2, full-shard) with gradient checkpointing. Final checkpoints are gathered and consolidated from the sharded (DTensor) state.

Training configuration. Unless noted, all methods train for 250250 update steps at a constant learning rate with the Adam optimizer in bf16, computing loss on assistant response tokens only. GRPO and OPD use 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}, and SPOT, SODA, and projected distillation use 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}. The per-step generation budget is matched at 88 rollouts: the distillation methods (OPD, SPOT, SODA, and ours) draw 88 problems per step, while GRPO draws a group of 88 samples on a single problem. The DPO-based objectives use β=0.1\beta{=}0.1; SODA runs a brief SFT warmup on y+y^{+} (first 2525 steps) before its preference phase. GRPO keeps TRL’s default KL coefficient of zero toward the reference policy.

C.2 Hard-Set Construction and Statistics

Mining rule. Training targets problems the student cannot already solve. For each candidate problem we draw k=16k{=}16 samples from the untrained student at temperature 0.80.8 (seed 00) and keep the problem only if all 1616 are graded wrong by that benchmark’s grader, i.e. pass@16=016=0. The retained problems form the frozen hard set; the 1616 failed samples are stored with each record, which is what allows an offline arm to be built without re-generating.

Because the criterion is defined against a specific student, hard sets are per student: the same benchmark yields a different hard set for Qwen3-8B than for OLMo-2-7B, and a checkpoint is only ever scored against the hard set mined for its own base model.

Tab. 6 reports the mining statistics for Qwen3-8B and Tab. 7 the split sizes for OLMo-2-7B. Hard-set size is a property of the student, not of the benchmark: GSM8K is hard for only 1.63%1.63\% of Qwen3-8B’s training pool, whereas MATH yields roughly twice as many hard problems for OLMo-2-7B (4,0464{,}046) as for Qwen3-8B (1,9911{,}991).

Train/evaluation disjointness. We verify rather than assume separation. Comparing question text lower-cased with LaTeX commands stripped and non-alphanumeric characters removed — so that a problem reformatted between two source releases is still caught, which a byte-level comparison would miss — gives zero overlap between hard set and evaluation slice for both math benchmarks: 1,9911{,}991 versus 500500 for MATH and 122122 versus 200200 for GSM8K. AMC23, MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) and HumanEval are evaluation-only and were never trained on by any method. Four problems appear twice inside the MATH hard set (1,9911{,}991 records, 1,9871{,}987 unique) and therefore carry double weight during training.

C.3 Prompt Templates

All prompts are single user turns passed through the model’s own chat template. For Qwen3 the thinking mode is disabled in mining, training and evaluation alike, so the same decoding regime holds throughout. The instruction appended to a question is selected by the benchmark’s answer type, which fixes the output format the grader expects; the grader always follows the evaluation benchmark, not the benchmark a checkpoint was trained on.

C.3.1 Student prompts

The student prompt is the question followed by one of the four instructions below.

Numeric (GSM8K):

Solve the problem by showing your full step-by-step reasoning. After the reasoning, write the final answer on a new line by itself in the exact format "#### N", where N is just the final number (no units, words, or commas). Always include this #### line as the last line.

Boxed (MATH, MATH-500, AMC23):

Solve the problem by showing your full step-by-step reasoning. Put your final answer inside \boxed{...} at the end. The content of the box must be exactly the final answer (a number or a simplified expression), with no surrounding words.

Multiple choice (SciKnowEval, MMLU):

Answer the multiple-choice question. Think step by step, then write the final answer on a new line by itself as "Answer: X" where X is A, B, C, or D.

Code (LiveCodeBench, HumanEval):

Complete the Python function. Return the full function definition inside a ```python code block. Do not include tests or explanation.

C.3.2 Projection prompt

The projector is instructed to edit the student’s wrong attempt rather than to solve the problem afresh; this is what keeps the target near the student’s own distribution and makes the token-level diff small. The role is set per domain (“expert math tutor” for numeric and boxed answers, “expert science tutor” for multiple choice, “expert assistant for tool/function calling” for tool use).

System message:

You are an {role}. A student answered a problem incorrectly. PROJECT their attempt onto a correct solution: keep the student’s overall approach, wording, and structure as much as possible, changing ONLY what is needed to make it correct. Do NOT rewrite from scratch in your own style --- stay as close to how the student writes as possible. {end-format requirement}

User message:

Problem:
{problem}
Student’s incorrect attempt:
{wrong attempt}
Minimally edit the student’s attempt into a correct solution, staying as close to their style as possible. {end-format requirement}

The end-format requirement names the graded target exactly: End with the correct final answer, {gold}. for math, the correct option for multiple choice, and the required Action / Action Input pair for tool calling. A projection that does not end in the graded format is rejected by the verifier, so a correction cannot be accepted on the strength of its prose alone; every accepted projection has been re-graded by the same grader used for evaluation.

Code is different in kind. For programming problems the correctness signal given to the projector is execution feedback on the student’s own attempt — which tests failed, with input, expected and actual values — and not the hidden test suite:

You are an expert competitive programmer helping a student. The student wrote a solution that FAILS some tests. PROJECT their attempt onto a correct one: keep the student’s overall approach, structure, and variable names as much as possible, changing ONLY what is needed to make it pass. Do NOT rewrite from scratch in your own style --- stay as close to how the student writes as possible. Return the corrected solution as a single code block.

C.4 Training Configuration: Additional Details

Sec. C.1 gives the models, learning rates, optimizer, per-step generation budget and hardware. This section records the details that a re-implementation additionally needs.

Generation budget per domain, and why it varies. The rollout budget must be at least the budget the hard set was mined with. A problem is in the hard set precisely because the student failed it under the mining budget, so giving the student a smaller budget during training truncates its derivation mid-proof and the problem cannot be solved even in principle. Competition MATH attempts run a median of roughly 805805 tokens, with 61%61\% needing at least 690690, so a 700700-token budget both pinned hard-set accuracy near zero and trained the model on truncated derivations, collapsing held-out accuracy from 0.390.39 to 0.160.16. The experiments of Sec. 4 therefore use a uniform 2,0482{,}048-token rollout budget, across both students and all five benchmarks, which is above the mining budget everywhere. Rollouts are sampled at T=0.8T{=}0.8. This is also why the mean deleted span reported for the gold arm in Tab. 15 exceeds 700700 tokens. The transfer runs of Sec. D.5 and the replication of Appendix I use their own budgets, stated in those sections.

Projector configuration. The black-box projector is Claude Opus 4.8, accessed through a hosted API and run off-GPU, which is what allows the whole pod to be spent on the student. Each wrong sample gets at most two projection attempts and the first verified-correct projection is kept; if neither verifies, the sample contributes no preference pair for that step. The same-family projector variant is served locally.

GPU allocation. Of the eight GPUs in the pod, seven hold FSDP2 shards of the student and one is reserved for the in-loop vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) generator that produces on-policy rollouts and runs the periodic evaluations. Sharing the generator GPU with a training rank starves the generator and stalls the step, so the split is fixed rather than dynamic.

Loss variants. The arms and their objectives are given in Appendix F. Two further switches are fixed throughout: the adopted default uses unnormalized rather than token-mean-normalized DPO log-probabilities, and the auxiliary SFT term acts on the student’s own correct rollouts ycy^{\mathrm{c}}, as in (2), not on the projection y+y^{+}.

C.5 Evaluation: Statistical Resolution and Seed Variance

Two kinds of seed. Two sources of variation are easy to conflate and differ by roughly a factor of fifty in magnitude.

  • •

    A training seed indexes an independently trained checkpoint. Different weights. The spread is large: the three math-trained projected-distillation seeds score 0.7490.749, 0.3110.311 and 0.6880.688 on MATH-500.

  • •

    An evaluation seed indexes which generations were sampled from one fixed checkpoint. The model is identical across replicates. The spread is small, typically ±0.006\pm 0.006 on the large suites.

The two are reported in different places. The ±\pm in Tabs. 11 and 12 is the standard error over evaluation seeds of a single training-seed-00 checkpoint: it certifies that a measurement would reproduce under re-sampling, and says nothing about whether a different training run would land near it. Everywhere else, including Tabs. 8, 9 and 10, the ±\pm is the standard error over the three training seeds. Claims about a method rather than about a particular checkpoint have to be read against training-seed spread, which is the dominant term.

Greedy decoding cannot be averaged this way. It is deterministic, so replicates return the same number and a standard deviation of exactly zero, which reports nothing about how well the mean is pinned down. Sampling one generation per problem and repeating over independent seeds gives an error bar that means something. For pass@kk estimated from n>kn>k samples we use the unbiased estimator of Chen et al. (2021), pass@​k=1−(n−ck)/(nk)\text{pass@}k=1-\binom{n-c}{k}\big/\binom{n}{k}. The pass@1616 figures in this paper are not estimated that way: they are computed from n=16n{=}16 draws as the share of problems solved at least once. That indicator is unbiased for pass@1616 when n=kn=k, but it carries more variance than an estimate from more draws would.

Resolution limits of the small suites. Suite size sets the granularity of any difference that can be claimed. AMC23 has only 4040 problems, so one problem is 0.0250.025 and the base standard error alone is ±0.030\pm 0.030; differences below roughly 0.060.06 there should not be argued. GSM8K (1,3191{,}319) and MMLU (14,04214{,}042) are the suites where small differences resolve.

A note on greedy reproducibility. Repeating a greedy evaluation with identical prompts and identical suite size did not return bit-identical scores. The cause is continuous-batching non-determinism in the inference server, which changes numerics enough to flip borderline argmax tokens. Greedy numbers therefore carry a small amount of unreported jitter of their own, which is a further reason to report a sampled mean with an explicit error bar.

Appendix D RQ1: Comparison with baselines

D.1 Metrics

Area under the Pareto frontier (AUPF). For a single run, evaluation at checkpoints i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n yields points (xi,yi)∈[0,1]2(x_{i},y_{i})\in[0,1]^{2}, where xix_{i} is specialization (hard-set pass@1) and yiy_{i} is retention (held-out pass@1). A point is dominated if another point is at least as good on both axes, and the Pareto frontier is the non-dominated set

ℱ={i:∄jwithxj≥xi,yj≥yi,(xj,yj)≠(xi,yi)}.\mathcal{F}=\bigl\{\,i:\ \nexists\,j\ \text{with}\ x_{j}\geq x_{i},\ y_{j}\geq y_{i},\ (x_{j},y_{j})\neq(x_{i},y_{i})\,\bigr\}. (3)

We anchor the frontier at a shared untrained base B=(0,H0)B=(0,H_{0}): specialization 00 and retention H0H_{0}, the untrained held-out accuracy, both estimated as the mean step-00 value over the methods that start untrained. Specialization at the anchor is measured at step 00 rather than inferred from the mining criterion; it averages 0.0120.012 across those methods, which we round to zero. BB is a forced left anchor (it is never subject to domination); using a shared base rather than each run’s own first checkpoint prevents methods that begin with an SFT warmup (e.g. SODA) from being scored against an already-elevated starting specialization. Indexing {B}∪ℱ\{B\}\cup\mathcal{F} in order of increasing specialization, 0=x~0<x~1<⋯<x~K0=\tilde{x}_{0}<\tilde{x}_{1}<\dots<\tilde{x}_{K}, AUPF is the area under the piecewise-linear frontier yℱ​(⋅)y_{\mathcal{F}}(\cdot) by the trapezoidal rule:

AUPF=∫0x~Kyℱ​(x)​𝑑x=∑k=1K12​(y~k−1+y~k)​(x~k−x~k−1).\mathrm{AUPF}\;=\;\int_{0}^{\tilde{x}_{K}}y_{\mathcal{F}}(x)\,dx\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\tfrac{1}{2}\,(\tilde{y}_{k-1}+\tilde{y}_{k})\,(\tilde{x}_{k}-\tilde{x}_{k-1}). (4)

We compute AUPF per seed and report the mean ±\pm s.e. across seeds. Because retention is integrated over specialization from the base at x=0x{=}0, a method that never specializes (x~K≈0\tilde{x}_{K}\!\approx\!0) has AUPF≈0\mathrm{AUPF}\!\approx\!0; a higher AUPF means pushing specialization further while holding retention.

Continual-learning metrics (Tab. 3). For a run with per-step specialization xtx_{t} and retention yty_{t} (t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T) and the shared untrained base (0,H0)(0,H_{0}), define

x¯\displaystyle\bar{x} =1T​∑t=1Txt,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{T}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}x_{t}, y¯\displaystyle\bar{y} =1T​∑t=1Tyt,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{T}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}y_{t},
BWT\displaystyle\mathrm{BWT} =yT−H0,\displaystyle=y_{T}-H_{0}, F\displaystyle F =maxτ≤T⁡yτ−yT​with​y0:=H0,\displaystyle=\max\nolimits_{\tau\leq T}y_{\tau}-y_{T}\ \text{with}\ y_{0}{:=}H_{0},
SafeSpecε\displaystyle\mathrm{SafeSpec}_{\varepsilon} =max⁡{xt:yt≥H0−ε},\displaystyle=\max\!\bigl\{x_{t}:y_{t}\geq H_{0}-\varepsilon\bigr\}, 00 if the set is empty.

x¯,y¯\bar{x},\bar{y} are training-averaged accuracies in the spirit of the AUC metrics of Kemker et al. (2018); BWT\mathrm{BWT} is the backward transfer of Lopez-Paz and Ranzato (2017) and FF the forgetting measure of Chaudhry et al. (2018). SafeSpecε\mathrm{SafeSpec}_{\varepsilon} is the highest specialization reached at any checkpoint whose retention is within ε\varepsilon of the untrained base. For the aggregate row in Tab. 3, retention is expressed as a fraction of base so panels with different retention scales are commensurate: y¯norm=y¯/H0\bar{y}_{\mathrm{norm}}=\bar{y}/H_{0}, Fnorm=F/H0F_{\mathrm{norm}}=F/H_{0}, BWTnorm=(yT−H0)/H0\mathrm{BWT}_{\mathrm{norm}}=(y_{T}-H_{0})/H_{0}, and pooled SafeSpec\mathrm{SafeSpec} uses yt/H0≥1−εrely_{t}/H_{0}\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} with εrel∈{0.02,0.05}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\in\{0.02,0.05\}. Each metric is computed per seed and averaged over 33 seeds; the aggregate pools further over ((family, benchmark)), with GRPO on Qwen-LiveCodeBench entered as no learning.

D.2 Per-cell results

Tab. 8 gives the exact final-checkpoint accuracies behind Fig. 3: hard-set pass@1 (specialization) and held-out pass@1 (retention), as mean ±\pm standard error across seeds at 250250 steps. Fig. 9 breaks that figure down per benchmark, Fig. 10 gives the pooled trajectories over training, and Tabs. 9 and 10 break the two continual-learning summaries of Tab. 3 down per cell.

D.3 Math-domain evaluation: in-domain and out-of-domain behavior

Sec. 4.1 measures retention on a held-out slice of the benchmark a method was trained on. Here we ask what training on one domain does to abilities elsewhere. For each math-trained Qwen3-8B method we evaluate its final checkpoint on five full test suites: GSM8K (1,3191{,}319 problems) and MATH-500 (500500) in the trained domain, and AMC23 (4040), MMLU (14,04214{,}042) and HumanEval (164164), none of which any method was trained on. The metric is sampled pass@1, one generation per problem at T=0.8T{=}0.8 and top-pp 0.950.95. Each evaluation is repeated with three evaluation seeds and averaged, with the checkpoint held fixed: an evaluation seed changes only which generations are sampled from that one model. The reported ±\pm is the standard error of that mean across the three replicates. Training and evaluation data are disjoint, with zero overlap between the 1,9911{,}991-problem math hard set and the 500500-problem evaluation slice on normalized, LaTeX-stripped text. Tab. 11 reports the absolute scores and Tab. 12 the change relative to the untrained student.

D.4 Discussion

Sec. 4.1 names three cells that go to a baseline; the full rows are in Tab. 8. On Qwen MATH, SODA reaches 0.1360.136 specialization at 0.6640.664 retention and SPOT 0.0870.087 at 0.2580.258, against our 0.0310.031 at 0.7600.760: both fit the hard set further than we do, and SPOT gives up most of its held-out accuracy doing so. On Qwen SciKnowEval, SODA reaches 0.2270.227 at 0.5730.573 against our 0.2040.204 at 0.4970.497, leading on both axes; our retention there carries a standard error of 0.1310.131 across seeds, against 0.0370.037 for SODA and 0.0040.004 for SPOT, so that cell is the least stable in the panel. On OLMo GSM8K, OPD reaches 0.4960.496 at 0.8030.803 against our 0.2360.236 at 0.8300.830.

The OLMo-2-7B LiveCodeBench cell is omitted from every RQ1 table and figure. No method moves specialization appreciably above zero there, so a frontier anchored at the base is degenerate and the cell contributes an area near zero for every method, our own included.

D.5 Transfer to other benchmarks’ hard problems

This subsection gives the setup and the full results of the transfer experiment summarized in Sec. 4.1 and Tab. 2.

Hard sets. For every problem of every pool we draw 1616 samples from the untrained Qwen3-8B at T=0.8T{=}0.8 (seed 00, thinking mode disabled, 3,0723{,}072 new tokens) and grade them with the MATH grader. A problem is hard when all 1616 are wrong, as in Sec. C.2. The budget is set so that a hard problem is one the student cannot solve rather than one it cannot finish (Sec. C.4). This leaves 628628 of the 11,99811{,}998 MATH training problems hard. We split the 628628 into 501501 training and 127127 held-out problems, stratified by subject and level. Every other pool is used only for testing. A test problem is removed when a MATH training problem covers at least 60%60\% of its 1313-word phrases with the same answer, which removes 410410 AIME and 474474 DAPO-Math problems.

Training and evaluation. Each method trains Qwen3-8B on the 501501 problems for 250250 updates (about four passes) with the configuration of Sec. C.1 and a 3,0723{,}072-token rollout budget, saving a checkpoint every 5050 updates, under one training seed. Ours, SPOT and SODA draw their corrections from the black-box projector, which corrects 1,7981{,}798 of our 1,8441{,}844 wrong attempts (97.5%97.5\%). The base model and every checkpoint draw 1616 samples per problem at T=0.8T{=}0.8 and top-pp 0.950.95 (seed 11, so the base scores slightly above zero on its own hard set); pass@1 is the mean over the samples and pass@16 the share of problems solved at least once. A change against the base is marked when it is at least twice its paired standard error. The four other benchmarks contribute 2,8852{,}885 hard problems in all, by benchmark in Tab. 13, out of 6,8746{,}874 that survive filtering and decontamination.

Which benchmarks transfer. Tab. 13 splits the cross-benchmark gain of our best checkpoint by benchmark. It concentrates in Omni-MATH and DAPO-Math, which together hold 2,5362{,}536 of the 2,8852{,}885 hard problems, and it holds under sampling and under greedy decoding alike. OlympiadBench moves within its standard error and the AIME problems do not move.

A second training benchmark. To check that the transfer is not specific to MATH, we repeat the experiment for our method with Omni-MATH as the training benchmark: 501501 of its 2,1782{,}178 hard problems, drawn in proportion to its difficulty levels and topics, and otherwise the same recipe and protocol. The projector corrects 8686 to 96%96\% of the wrong attempts. The two runs share most test problems, so Tab. 14 compares them on identical sets: the 127127 held-out MATH hard problems, the 1,6771{,}677 Omni-MATH hard problems that neither run trained on, and the three benchmarks that neither run trained on (OlympiadBench, AIME 1983–2023 and DAPO-Math). Transfer runs in both directions and to a similar degree. Training on Omni-MATH lifts the held-out MATH hard problems about as much as training on MATH does (pass@16 0.3620.362 against 0.3540.354), and training on MATH lifts the Omni-MATH hard problems nearly as much as training on Omni-MATH does (pass@1 0.0180.018 against 0.0220.022). The Omni-MATH run transfers more to the three olympiad-style benchmarks (0.0300.030 against 0.0240.024). The direction of training therefore does not decide where the gain appears.

Appendix E RQ2: Edit size

E.1 Setup and measurement

Qwen3-8B student, GSM8K hard set (mined pass@kk==00, 122122 problems), black-box projector, one objective shared by every arm, lr 1​e−51\mathrm{e}{-}5, β=0.1\beta{=}0.1, 250250 steps, 33 seeds. The axis is realized by edit magnitude: the minimal edit, then re-prompting the projector for progressively larger rewrites of the same attempt, plus the student-agnostic gold anchor. Because the projector rather than the prompt determines how much text it actually replaces, arms are identified by their measured edit size (Tab. 15); the two larger arms realize 3.2×3.2\times and 3.9×3.9\times the minimal edit. Off-policyness is the log-likelihood difference between the correction and the attempt under the current student πθ\pi_{\theta},

Λ=log⁡πθ​(y+∣x)−log⁡πθ​(y−∣x),\Lambda\;=\;\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{+}\mid x)\;-\;\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{-}\mid x), (5)

and a larger |Λ||\Lambda| means the correction sits farther from what the student would itself produce. We summarize Λ\Lambda by its median over training steps rather than its mean: the per-step quantity is heavy-tailed, since a rollout is scored against a policy that has advanced by up to five optimizer steps since it was sampled, and occasional large excursions dominate an average. The median is stable across seeds (Tab. 15) whereas the mean is not. For gold, which replaces a long attempt with a short reference solution, Λ\Lambda moves chiefly through length; Tab. 15 reports its value with that caveat, and it is omitted from the |Λ||\Lambda| panel of Fig. 4.

E.2 Ablation arms

Tab. 15 lists the per-arm endpoint accuracies with the off-policyness scalar |Λ||\Lambda| and the mean edit-span sizes |E+|,|E−||E^{+}|,|E^{-}| that define the arms. Both spans grow together across the edit arms, so the two are not separable here. gold is the exception in kind rather than in degree, inserting the fewest tokens of any arm while deleting the entire attempt.

E.3 Mechanism

Full-utterance and diff-localized shift. Fig. 11 compares Λ\Lambda measured over the whole utterance against the same quantity restricted to the changed spans E−/E+E^{-}\!/E^{+}. The two agree at r=0.9999r=0.9999 across all 2,2492{,}249 logged steps of the edit arms, with the localized quantity retaining 9494 to 95%95\% of the magnitude, because the tokens before the first edit are both identical and identically conditioned, so their contributions cancel exactly. Shared tokens after an edit do not: they are scored on prefixes that have already diverged, and they are what the remaining 55 to 6%6\% measures. Localizing the measurement, as the objective of (1) does, therefore keeps almost all of the signal.

Edit size and the likelihood shift, step by step. Fig. 12 plots every logged step of the edit arms, with the edit size realized at that step against the likelihood shift it demands. The relation is strongly monotone but not linear. Pooling the arms, the median |Λ||\Lambda| rises across every edit-size decile, from 8282 in the smallest to 570570 in the largest (Spearman ρ=0.83\rho=0.83), while the Pearson correlation is only 0.280.28. Both concavity and a heavy tail depress it, and the tail dominates: dropping the largest 2%2\% of |Λ||\Lambda| raises Pearson to 0.710.71, whereas linearizing the concavity alone, by correlating against log⁡|Λ|\log|\Lambda|, reaches 0.500.50. The effect also diminishes with the size of the edit: the per-step Theil–Sen slope is 0.720.72 [0.630.63, 0.820.82] at the minimal edit against 0.170.17 [0.160.16, 0.180.18] and 0.140.14 [0.130.13, 0.150.15] at the two larger rewrites, and the relation holds within each arm on its own (ρ=0.52\rho=0.52, 0.820.82, 0.780.78). We therefore read edit size as a monotone indicator of the likelihood shift rather than a proportional one.

Insertion and deletion across the arms. Fig. 13 reports the per-step ratio |E+|/|E−||E^{+}|/|E^{-}|. It falls monotonically along the axis, from 2.462.46 at the minimal edit through 1.331.33 and 0.990.99 at the larger rewrites to 0.130.13 for gold, so what changes across the arms is not only the amount rewritten but whether the correction predominantly adds to the attempt or replaces it.

The two edit-size measures. That asymmetry is also what separates the quantity Sec. 4.2 reports from the one Theorem 1 uses. Tab. 16 gives both for every arm.

E.4 Additional results

Specialization–retention plane. Fig. 14 plots the two axes against each other. The minimal edit occupies the upper-right region, dominating both larger rewrites on both axes, while gold attains intermediate specialization at the lowest retention of any arm.

Held-out trajectory. Fig. 15 tracks held-out accuracy over training. The edit arms separate in edit-size order and decline smoothly, the minimal edit holding near its base value throughout. gold instead destabilizes early, falling to 0.540.54 by step 7575 and remaining volatile for the rest of the run before settling at 0.7440.744.

Appendix F RQ4: Loss-recipe details

F.1 Objectives

Rollout terminology. Each training step, the student rolls out attempts on the hard problems and the verifier splits them: a correct rollout ycy^{\mathrm{c}} is one it solves on its own (R⁡(x,yc)=1R(x,y^{\mathrm{c}})=1); a wrong rollout y−y^{-} is one it fails (R=0R=0). For each wrong rollout the frozen projector produces the minimal-edit projection y+y^{+} (verified-correct, Sec. 3), and a token-diff aligns (y−,y+)(y^{-},y^{+}) into the mistake span E−E^{-} and fix span E+E^{+} used by (1). The full-sequence DPO variant replaces E+,E−E^{+},E^{-} in (1) with the full sequences y+,y−y^{+},y^{-}.

Per-arm objectives. The four contrastive arms optimize ℒDPOE\mathcal{L}^{E}_{\mathrm{DPO}} (diff-local, on the changed spans E±E^{\pm}) or ℒDPOseq\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{\mathrm{DPO}} (full-sequence, on y±y^{\pm}), each with or without an added self-SFT term ℒSFT​(yc)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y^{\mathrm{c}}) on the student’s own correct rollouts. RFT optimizes ℒSFT​(yc)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y^{\mathrm{c}}) alone (no projected target, no contrast); SFT on projection ++ self-SFT optimizes ℒSFT​(y+)+ℒSFT​(yc)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y^{+})+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(y^{\mathrm{c}}) (SFT on the projected correction y+y^{+} plus self-SFT on the student’s own correct rollouts, no contrast).

F.2 Results

Compute (batch size), number of epochs and learning rate are matched across arms. Tab. 17 gives the absolute numbers behind Fig. 6.

Three things the table does not show. RFT is limited by how rarely the student succeeds unaided: the hard set is mined at pass​@​k=0\mathrm{pass}@k{=}0, and its rollouts stay correct on about 6%6\% of attempts through the run, so it trains on very little. The instability of SFT on the projection runs across both axes, its standard error of 0.0780.078 on specialization and 0.0540.054 on retention being three to sixteen and four to twenty-seven times those of any other arm. And the self-SFT term is worth +0.082+0.082 to the full-sequence contrast and +0.161+0.161 to the diff-local one in absolute pass@1: because the projection edits few tokens, a full-sequence contrast is spread over spans that are already correct while a diff-local one acts only where the edit fell, and that concentration leaves it with less absolute signal of its own, so it gains more from a term that raises the likelihood of correct text outright.

Appendix G RQ5: Refinement details

G.1 Refinement protocol

A correction is valid only if a reasoning check confirms that its derivation process actually yields the answer, so a projection that reaches the right answer by an unsound route is discarded. Round 00 is a single correction pass. In each subsequent round the frozen projector is re-prompted with its own previous correction together with the spans it edited in that correction, and returns a refined correction. Across rounds we keep the valid correction that the student itself is most likely to produce, scored by the base student’s log-likelihood on the edited tokens, which selects for corrections the student can absorb rather than for the ones the projector prefers. The projector is never updated. All arms train the Qwen3-8B student for 250250 steps with the default recipe of Sec. 3 over 33 seeds.

G.2 Results

Projection quality. Refinement improves the corrections on three counts at once, and the three are linked. Re-prompting the projector with the spans it has already edited pushes it to consolidate rather than rewrite, so the correction it returns reaches the right answer more often and departs from the student’s own attempt less: the median |Λ||\Lambda| falls from 38.138.1 to 26.226.2 over the two rounds, placing the refined targets nearer the student in the sense Sec. 4.2 measures, and the edit size falls with it. The K=0K{=}0 edit size carries a standard error of 7070 tokens across seeds, so the level of that row is the least settled number in the table; the ordering across budgets is what the comparison rests on.

Downstream trade-off. Fig. 16 traces the attainable frontier over training for each budget. Refinement extends it: the furthest specialization reached on the frontier rises from 0.3930.393 at K=0K{=}0 to 0.4590.459 at K=1K{=}1 and 0.4750.475 at K=2K{=}2. The K=2K{=}2 frontier also lies above the other two over the whole sweep, and is the only one that rises above the shared base in retention, reaching 0.9600.960 against the base’s 0.9550.955, while K=0K{=}0 and K=1K{=}1 only decline from it; the extension in specialization is therefore not paid for out of retention. At the final checkpoint (Tab. 18) the two budgets that refine are level on specialization and K=2K{=}2 holds retention slightly higher; against standard errors of 0.0100.010–0.0210.021 neither difference is resolved, and what separates the three budgets is the first round.

Correction rate over training. Fig. 17 shows the per-step correction rate for K∈{0,1,2}K\in\{0,1,2\}. For every KK the rate rises early and then declines as training proceeds, because the student learns the easily-correctable problems and the wrong attempts that remain in later training are the hardest ones, which even the refined projector rarely corrects. The main-text Fig. 7 reports the running (cumulative) version of this quantity.

Appendix H RQ6: Self-projection details

Everywhere else in this paper the projector is a separate and stronger model. Here we make the same model write the correction. We give the student its own wrong attempt together with privileged information, the verified final answer, and ask it for a correct solution that stays close to what it wrote. That output is then used exactly as a projector’s correction would be, with the same objective and the same training loop. Nothing else changes, so the run measures how much of the method depends on the projector being stronger than the student.

The student is Qwen3-8B and the hard set is the 122122 GSM8K problems it fails on all 1616 attempts. The teacher is a frozen copy of the student’s own base weights, so it does not improve as the student does. We train for 250250 updates over 33 seeds, with the same data, budget and evaluation as the edit-size runs of Sec. 4.2, from which the reference rows are taken. The answer is supplied with an instruction to derive it rather than assert it; without that, the model appends the answer line to unchanged wrong reasoning and the grader accepts it. We also run the same idea at the logit level, where the frozen base model scores the student’s own generation under a prompt carrying the answer and the student trains on that token distribution instead of on edited text.

Self-projection works, but it does not match a stronger projector. It lifts the hard set from 0.0000.000 to 0.2190.219 while retention stays at 0.9240.924, so an 8B model that is told the answer can repair its own reasoning often enough to learn from it. A black-box projector reaches 0.5600.560 on the same problems, and even the gold solution reaches 0.4890.489. Self-projection recovers about 40%40\% of the specialization, which says that the projector’s strength, and not the privileged answer by itself, is what the method mostly relies on.

The logit version gives almost nothing, 0.0460.046 after 250250 updates. The answer does reach the teacher, and the student never sees it, so the two token distributions differ from the first step; what is missing is not information but capability. The teacher is the student’s own base weights, and being told which answer is correct does not let those weights produce a correct derivation, so the distribution it supplies over the student’s own tokens carries little the student can use. The measured loss stays between 0.0030.003 and 0.0060.006 throughout, and making the target denser, a pure forward KL against the teacher’s top-2020 tokens rather than its top-11, roughly doubled the result from a very small base.

Two points help in reading the table. The text-level and logit-level arms inherit different learning rates from their respective families in the main experiments (10−510^{-5} and 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}), so each is comparable to its own column rather than to the other; the comparison against the black-box projector is at a matched 10−510^{-5}. The 8B also does not edit minimally. It appends a fresh derivation rather than repairing the attempt, which is part of why it falls short: producing a small, targeted edit is precisely what the weaker projector cannot do.

Appendix I Comparison with concurrent self-projection

Concurrent work (Karan et al., 2026) also moves the supervision toward the student, but does so by self-projection: an MCMC sampler in which the student itself, shown the problem, a reference solution and a partial response, regenerates the response block by block (3232 blocks of 5858 tokens, 1010 proposals per block), accepting a proposal when it raises the student’s mean log-likelihood. The student is then fine-tuned on the resulting traces (Sampling SFT), optionally followed by GRPO (Sampling SFT + RL). We reproduce the math setting of that work’s Table 1 with its released code, data, training recipes and evaluation scripts, and change only where the correction comes from: the black-box projector minimally edits each wrong attempt given the reference answer (Sec. C.3), and that work’s grader must accept the edit.

Setup. The student is Qwen2.5-3B, trained on that work’s 7,9627{,}962 MATH training problems. It answers each once with that work’s prompt (T=0.6T{=}0.6, 1,8561{,}856 tokens) and solves 3,6753{,}675; the projector corrects 4,2654{,}265 of the other 4,2874{,}287 attempts within two tries (4,3174{,}317 calls, 11.211.2M tokens). We train four arms from these data, one training seed each:

  • •

    Black-box projection + SFT: that work’s SFT recipe (learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, 22 epochs, batch 1616, cosine schedule with 1010 warm-up steps, sequences up to 2,0482{,}048 tokens) on the 3,6753{,}675 correct answers and the 4,2654{,}265 projections, in place of its MCMC traces.

  • •

    Black-box projection + SFT + RL: that work’s RL stage on the previous arm (GRPO for 500500 updates of 256256 problems ×\times 44 rollouts, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, KL coefficient 0.0010.001).

  • •

    Ours, static pool: the objective of (2) on the same data, the 4,2654{,}265 pairs (y−,y+)(y^{-},y^{+}) supplying the contrast and the 3,6753{,}675 correct answers the self-SFT term, for 1,9851{,}985 updates of 88 records (22 passes, as for SFT) at learning rate 10−510^{-5}. As in Sec. 4.3, the corrections are mined once against the untrained student.

  • •

    Ours, online refresh: the full recipe of Sec. 3, in which every update samples the current student on 88 problems and projects its wrong answers, for 250250 updates.

Evaluation follows that work’s protocol: one sample per problem at T=0.6T{=}0.6 with up to 1,8561{,}856 tokens, on MATH levels 33–55 (1,0241{,}024 problems), AMC (8383), MATH-500 (500500) and GSM8K (1,3201{,}320) for the trained skill, and on SciKnowEval chemistry (600600) and MMLU (lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024b), 00-shot) for prior capabilities. Our SFT ran in TRL rather than verl (Sheng et al., 2024), with the same settings.

Findings. SFT on black-box projections reaches a math average of 0.5450.545 against 0.5340.534 for Sampling SFT, and 0.5790.579 against 0.5670.567 once the same RL stage is added (Tab. 20). Within our own runs, the objective of (2) on the static pool beats SFT on the same data (0.5570.557 against 0.5450.545; +0.039±0.014+0.039\pm 0.014 on MATH(3,4,5)) and matches SFT + RL on MATH(3,4,5) to within noise, at 1/241/24 of its compute (Tab. 21). Prior capabilities hold for every arm: MMLU stays within 0.0060.006 of base, and no change in Chemistry is significant.

Two features of this setting bear on the online arm. The static pool covers 7,9627{,}962 problems and is passed over only twice, so it never reaches the regime in which a pool has been reused for several rounds, which is where the static arm of Sec. 4.3 falls; and the online run trains on an eighth as many records. Under these conditions the static pool scores higher (0.5570.557 against 0.5270.527).

Compute. The MCMC sampler accounts for 98%98\% of Sampling SFT’s compute: each proposal re-reads a 521521-token prompt, regenerates part of the response and is re-scored, about 2.5×1052.5\times 10^{5} token passes per training problem. Black-box projection uses at least 30×30\times less compute on the student’s hardware. The RL stage costs about as much as the whole MCMC step, so it dominates both arms that include it.

Appendix J Theoretical analysis

J.1 The Patch MDP: Model and Assumption

This appendix gives the model and the assumption behind Sec. 5; Sec. J.2 gives the proofs.

Definition 2 (Patch MDP).

We define a patch MDP as the tuple ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,p,r,ρ,γ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,r,\rho,\gamma) over a vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V} with token budget HH:

  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S}: a state is a full history s=(x,y′)s=(x,y^{\prime}), a problem together with the tokens y′y^{\prime} generated so far; st=(x,y1:t)s_{t}=(x,y_{1:t}) is the state before decision tt, and |s||s| counts the generated tokens.

  • •

    𝒜\mathcal{A}: an action is a patch, a token span fitting the remaining budget, 𝒜⁡(s)={w∈𝒱h:1≤h≤H−|s|}\mathcal{A}(s)=\{w\in\mathcal{V}^{h}:1\leq h\leq H-|s|\}.

  • •

    pp: transitions are deterministic and append the patch, p⁡(s⊕w∣s,w)=1p(s\oplus w\mid s,w)=1.

  • •

    rr: the reward is token-additive, r⁡(s,w)=∑j=1|w|rtok​(s⊕w<j,wj)r(s,w)=\sum_{j=1}^{|w|}r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j}) with rtok∈[0,1]r_{\mathrm{tok}}\in[0,1], so a rollout returns at most HH.

  • •

    ρ\rho: the initial state distribution is the distribution over problems, s0=(x,∅)s_{0}=(x,\varnothing) with x∼ρx\sim\rho.

  • •

    γ=1\gamma=1: no discounting. 𝒱\mathcal{V} contains a terminal symbol, and a rollout that emits it moves to an absorbing state of zero reward and zero value.

Each decision emits one token, so a rollout takes exactly HH of them, indexed t=0,…,H−1t=0,\dots,H-1 with sHs_{H} absorbing. Then dπ(s)=1H∑t=0H−1Prπ[st=s]d^{\pi}(s)=\tfrac{1}{H}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\Pr_{\pi}[s_{t}=s] is a probability distribution over states, the normalized occupancy of π\pi.

Write V⋆V^{\star} and Q⋆Q^{\star} for the optimal value and action-value of ℳ\mathcal{M}. The return of a policy and its optimum are

J⁡(π)=𝔼s0∼ρ​𝔼π​[∑t=0H−1rtok​(st,wt)],J⋆=maxπ⁡J⁡(π)=𝔼s0∼ρ​[V⋆​(s0)],J(\pi)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s_{t},w_{t})\Big],\qquad J^{\star}\;=\;\max_{\pi}J(\pi)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho}\big[V^{\star}(s_{0})\big], (6)

the second equality because an optimal policy is optimal from every state.

Definition 3 (Optimality gap).

Δ⁡(s,w)≔V⋆​(s)−Q⋆​(s,w)\Delta(s,w)\coloneqq V^{\star}(s)-Q^{\star}(s,w) is the return an action forfeits against the best one available at ss, and Δmax≔sups,wΔ⁡(s,w)\Delta_{\max}\coloneqq\sup_{s,w}\Delta(s,w), finite because returns lie in [0,H][0,H]. It is a constant of ℳ\mathcal{M}, and plays the role of the cost-to-go constant uu of Ross et al. (2011).

Definition 4 (Edit count and edit size).

For histories s,s′s,s^{\prime},

e⁡(s,s′)≔|s|+|s′|−2​|LCS⁡(s,s′)|,e(s,s^{\prime})\;\coloneqq\;|s|+|s^{\prime}|-2\,\big|\mathrm{LCS}(s,s^{\prime})\big|,

where LCS⁡(s,s′)\mathrm{LCS}(s,s^{\prime}) is a longest common subsequence (Hirschberg, 1975) of their generated tokens. This counts the insertions and deletions carrying one into the other, the string-to-string correction distance of Wagner and Fischer (1974) restricted to those two operations. The edit size of a correction is m≔e⁡(y−,y+)m\coloneqq e(y^{-},y^{+}), the two rollouts compared at the HH decisions Definition 2 gives them, absorbing padding included. It exceeds the token-diff count |E−|+|E+||E^{-}|+|E^{+}| of Sec. 3, which Sec. 4.2 measures, by exactly the change in answer length: m=|E−|+|E+|+||y−|−|y+||m=|E^{-}|+|E^{+}|+\big|\,|y^{-}|-|y^{+}|\,\big|.

The learning problem.

Training runs for MM rounds. In round ii the learner πi\pi_{i} samples rollouts, a frozen projector rewrites the wrong ones, and the learner is scored on those rewrites and updated once. The learner ranges over a policy class Π={πθ:θ∈Θ}\Pi=\{\pi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} with Θ⊆ℝd\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} convex of Euclidean diameter DD, so minimizing over π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and over θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta are the same operation; only Proposition 1 uses this.

Where the loss is read.

The learner corrects a whole rollout once and scores the correction in a single forward pass, so the loss is evaluated at corrected prefixes, not at the states the learner visits. Write d~i(s~)=1H∑t=0H−1Pr[s~t=s~]\tilde{d}_{i}(\tilde{s})=\tfrac{1}{H}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\Pr[\tilde{s}_{t}=\tilde{s}] for the occupancy of those corrected prefixes in round ii, the state-visitation distribution the loss is read under and the counterpart of dπid^{\pi_{i}}. For any distribution dd over states, let

L(d,π)≔𝔼s∼d𝔼w∼π(⋅∣s)[Δ(s,w)]L(d,\pi)\;\coloneqq\;\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d}\,\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)}\big[\Delta(s,w)\big] (7)

be the mean gap of π\pi under dd. Performance is controlled by L⁡(dπi,πi)L(d^{\pi_{i}},\pi_{i}), but the algorithm can only reduce L⁡(d~i,π)L(\tilde{d}_{i},\pi).

The projector.

The projector edits a wrong attempt into a correct one, and w⋆​(s)w^{\star}(s) denotes its token at ss. We idealize it as an expert: its token is optimal wherever we read it, so Δ⁡(s,w⋆​(s))=0\Delta(s,w^{\star}(s))=0. Corollary 2 gives the bound for a projector that is suboptimal.

Definition 5 (Surrogate, realizability, average regret).

The surrogate objective ε~i​(π)\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi) for policy π\pi is the 00–11 disagreement with the projector, measured under d~i\tilde{d}_{i}:

ε~i(π)≔𝔼s~∼d~i[Prw∼π(⋅∣s~)[w≠w⋆(s~)]]=𝔼s~∼d~i[ 1−π(w⋆(s~)∣s~)].\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi)\;\coloneqq\;\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{s}\sim\tilde{d}_{i}}\Big[\Pr_{w\sim\pi(\cdot\mid\tilde{s})}\big[w\neq w^{\star}(\tilde{s})\big]\Big]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{s}\sim\tilde{d}_{i}}\big[\,1-\pi(w^{\star}(\tilde{s})\mid\tilde{s})\,\big].

The approximation and optimization terms are

ε~≔minπ∈Π⁡1M​∑i=1Mε~i​(π),γ~M≔1M​(∑i=1Mε~i​(πi)−min⁡∑i=1Mπ∈Π⁡ε~i​(π)),\tilde{\varepsilon}\;\coloneqq\;\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi),\qquad\tilde{\gamma}_{M}\;\coloneqq\;\frac{1}{M}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{i})-\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi)\Big),

so that 1M​∑iε~i​(πi)=ε~+γ~M\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{i})=\tilde{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}_{M} and the learner is no-regret when γ~M→0\tilde{\gamma}_{M}\to 0. Here ε~\tilde{\varepsilon} is a minimum over the policy class, so it measures how well the class can reproduce the projector’s tokens. It is unaffected by how much return those tokens forfeit; that enters separately, as δ¯\bar{\delta} in Corollary 2.

J.1.1 The assumption

The analysis rests on Assumption 1, stated in Sec. 5: the map s↦𝔼w∼π(⋅∣s)[Δ(s,w)]s\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)}[\Delta(s,w)] is η\eta-Lipschitz in the edit count e⁡(⋅,⋅)e(\cdot,\cdot), uniformly over π∈Π\pi\in\Pi. It is the only assumption the analysis makes about the MDP. Three points about it follow.

The Lipschitz constant is uniform over Π\Pi and over pairs of histories, but the proof invokes it only at the pairs (st,s~t)(s_{t},\tilde{s}_{t}) that Lemma 4 compares, so η\eta may be taken as the largest shift over those pairs.

The condition is placed on the averaged gap rather than on Δ⁡(s,w)\Delta(s,w) at a fixed ww. The proof compares 𝔼w∼π​[Δ]\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi}[\Delta] at two different prefixes, and moving from one to the other shifts the action distribution as well as the gap, so both must be controlled. Two pointwise conditions suffice. Suppose the gap is itself Lipschitz, |Δ⁡(s′,w)−Δ⁡(s,w)|≤ηΔ​e​(s,s′)|\Delta(s^{\prime},w)-\Delta(s,w)|\leq\eta_{\Delta}\,e(s,s^{\prime}), and the policy is smooth in the same count, TV(π(⋅∣s),π(⋅∣s′))≤κe(s,s′)\mathrm{TV}\big(\pi(\cdot\mid s),\pi(\cdot\mid s^{\prime})\big)\leq\kappa\,e(s,s^{\prime}). Adding and subtracting 𝔼w∼π(⋅∣s′)[Δ(s,w)]\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s^{\prime})}[\Delta(s,w)] splits the difference in two, bounded by ηΔ​e\eta_{\Delta}e and, since Δ\Delta takes values in [0,Δmax][0,\Delta_{\max}] and its oscillation is therefore at most Δmax\Delta_{\max}, by Δmax​κ​e\Delta_{\max}\kappa e. Together they give Assumption 1 with η≤ηΔ+Δmax​κ\eta\leq\eta_{\Delta}+\Delta_{\max}\kappa.

Assumption 1 is also the only reason any result below depends on the size of an edit. An argument that knows only which decisions sit downstream of an edit pays Δmax\Delta_{\max} at each of them, which is identical for a one-token edit and for a hundred-token edit at the same position: “the prefix differs” is a binary predicate and it saturates. Assumption 1 instead charges in proportion to e⁡(⋅,⋅)e(\cdot,\cdot), which every edit-size claim below uses.

J.2 Proofs

J.2.1 The gap decomposes across a patch

Lemma 1 (Patch additivity).

For patch MDP, Δ(s,w1:h)=∑j=1hΔ(s⊕w<j,wj)\ \Delta(s,w_{1:h})=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\Delta(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j}).

Proof.

Since the transitions of Patch MDP are deterministic (c.f. Definition 2), Q⋆(s,w1:h)=r(s,w1:h)+V⋆(s⊕w1:h)Q^{\star}(s,w_{1:h})=r(s,w_{1:h})+V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{1:h}), and by Definition 2 the reward splits as r(s,w1:h)=∑j=1hrtok(s⊕w<j,wj)r(s,w_{1:h})=\sum_{j=1}^{h}r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j}). Hence

Δ(s,w1:h)\displaystyle\Delta(s,w_{1:h}) =V⋆(s)−r(s,w1:h)−V⋆(s⊕w1:h)\displaystyle=V^{\star}(s)-r(s,w_{1:h})-V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{1:h}) (by determinism)
=V⋆(s)−V⋆(s⊕w1:h)−∑j=1hrtok(s⊕w<j,wj)\displaystyle=V^{\star}(s)-V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{1:h})-\sum_{j=1}^{h}r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j}) (by Definition 2)
=∑j=1h[V⋆​(s⊕w<j)−V⋆​(s⊕w<j+1)]−∑j=1hrtok​(s⊕w<j,wj)\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\big[V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{<j})-V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{<j+1})\big]-\sum_{j=1}^{h}r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j}) (telescoping)
=∑j=1h[V⋆​(s⊕w<j)−rtok​(s⊕w<j,wj)−V⋆​(s⊕w<j+1)]\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\big[V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{<j})-r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j})-V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{<j+1})\big]

where the last step uses Q⋆​(s⊕w<j,wj)=rtok​(s⊕w<j,wj)+V⋆​(s⊕w<j+1)Q^{\star}(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j})=r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s\oplus w_{<j},w_{j})+V^{\star}(s\oplus w_{<j+1}). ∎

The total gap along a rollout is therefore the same however the rollout is cut into patches; only the per-step decomposition changes.

J.2.2 Regret is the accumulated gap, under the learner’s own occupancy

Lemma 2 (No distribution shift).

Under Definition 2, for every round ii,

J⋆−J⁡(πi)=𝔼πi​[∑t=0H−1Δ⁡(st,wt)]=H​L​(dπi,πi),J^{\star}-J(\pi_{i})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{i}}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\Delta(s_{t},w_{t})\Big]\;=\;H\,L(d^{\pi_{i}},\pi_{i}),

Proof.

Fix one trajectory (s0,w0,…,sH−1,wH−1)(s_{0},w_{0},\dots,s_{H-1},w_{H-1}) generated by πi\pi_{i}. By Definition 2 it has exactly HH decisions and V⋆​(sH)=0V^{\star}(s_{H})=0, since sHs_{H} is the absorbing state with zero value. Then

V⋆​(s0)−∑t=0H−1rtok​(st,wt)\displaystyle V^{\star}(s_{0})-\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s_{t},w_{t}) =∑t=0H−1[V⋆​(st)−rtok​(st,wt)−V⋆​(st+1)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\big[V^{\star}(s_{t})-r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s_{t},w_{t})-V^{\star}(s_{t+1})\big] (telescoping, V⋆​(sH)=0V^{\star}(s_{H})=0)
=∑t=0H−1Δ⁡(st,wt)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\Delta(s_{t},w_{t}) (Q⋆​(st,wt)=rtok​(st,wt)+V⋆​(st+1)Q^{\star}(s_{t},w_{t})=r_{\mathrm{tok}}(s_{t},w_{t})+V^{\star}(s_{t+1}))

𝔼πi​[∑t=0H−1Δ⁡(st,wt)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{i}}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\Delta(s_{t},w_{t})\Big] =∑t=0H−1𝔼⁡[Δ⁡(st,wt)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}\big[\Delta(s_{t},w_{t})\big] (exactly HH terms, by Definition 2)
=H​𝔼s∼dπi​𝔼w∼πi​[Δ⁡(s,w)]\displaystyle=H\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi_{i}}}\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi_{i}}\big[\Delta(s,w)\big] (by the definition of dπid^{\pi_{i}})
=H​L​(dπi,πi)\displaystyle=H\,L(d^{\pi_{i}},\pi_{i})

∎

Both expectations in L⁡(dπi,πi)L(d^{\pi_{i}},\pi_{i}) are taken under πi\pi_{i}’s own occupancy. No change of measure is performed, so no concentrability coefficient appears.

J.2.3 Disagreement with the projector dominates the gap

Lemma 3 (Reduction).

Under Definition 3, with the projector idealized as above, for every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and every round ii,

L⁡(d~i,π)≤Δmax​ε~i​(π).L(\tilde{d}_{i},\pi)\;\leq\;\Delta_{\max}\,\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi).
Proof.

Fix a corrected state s~\tilde{s} and split the expectation over the projector’s token and the rest:

𝔼w∼π​[Δ​(s~,w)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi}\big[\Delta(\tilde{s},w)\big] =π⁡(w⋆∣s~)​Δ​(s~,w⋆)+∑w≠w⋆π⁡(w∣s~)​Δ​(s~,w)\displaystyle=\pi(w^{\star}\mid\tilde{s})\,\Delta(\tilde{s},w^{\star})+\sum_{w\neq w^{\star}}\pi(w\mid\tilde{s})\,\Delta(\tilde{s},w)
=∑w≠w⋆π⁡(w∣s~)​Δ​(s~,w)\displaystyle=\sum_{w\neq w^{\star}}\pi(w\mid\tilde{s})\,\Delta(\tilde{s},w) (Δ⁡(s~,w⋆)=0\Delta(\tilde{s},w^{\star})=0, idealized projector)
≤Δmax​∑w≠w⋆π⁡(w∣s~)\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{\max}\sum_{w\neq w^{\star}}\pi(w\mid\tilde{s}) (by Definition 3)
=Δmax​(1−π⁡(w⋆∣s~))\displaystyle=\Delta_{\max}\big(1-\pi(w^{\star}\mid\tilde{s})\big)

Taking 𝔼s~∼d~i\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{s}\sim\tilde{d}_{i}} of both sides and applying Definition 5 gives the claim. ∎

This is the reduction of Ross et al. (2011), applied at the corrected prefixes rather than at the learner’s own states.

J.2.4 Transfer from the corrected prefixes to the learner’s own

Lemma 4 (Transfer).

Under Assumption 1 and Definition 2, for every round ii,

L⁡(dπi,πi)≤L⁡(d~i,πi)+η​e¯i,where​e¯i≔𝔼i​[1H​∑t=0H−1et]L(d^{\pi_{i}},\pi_{i})\;\leq\;L(\tilde{d}_{i},\pi_{i})+\eta\,\bar{e}_{i},~\textit{where}~\bar{e}_{i}\;\coloneqq\;\mathbb{E}_{i}\Big[\tfrac{1}{H}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}e_{t}\Big]

and et≔e⁡(st,s~t)e_{t}\coloneqq e(s_{t},\tilde{s}_{t}) is the edit count between the learner’s own prefix at decision tt and the corrected prefix at that decision. A round draws one problem, one rollout of πi\pi_{i} on it, and the one correction the projector returns for that rollout; 𝔼i\mathbb{E}_{i} is the average over that draw.

Proof.

Pair the two distributions decision by decision: the tt-th term pairs the learner’s own prefix sts_{t} with the corrected prefix s~t\tilde{s}_{t}, which differ by ete_{t} tokens (Definition 4). By Definition 2 both sides of (7) are averages of exactly HH such terms, so

L⁡(dπi,πi)\displaystyle L(d^{\pi_{i}},\pi_{i}) =1H∑t=0H−1𝔼i𝔼w∼πi(⋅∣st)[Δ(st,w)]\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{H}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}_{i}\,\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid s_{t})}\big[\Delta(s_{t},w)\big] (by Definition 2)
≤1H∑t=0H−1𝔼i[𝔼w∼πi(⋅∣s~t)[Δ(s~t,w)]+ηet]\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{1}{H}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}_{i}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid\tilde{s}_{t})}\big[\Delta(\tilde{s}_{t},w)\big]+\eta\,e_{t}\Big] (by Assumption 1)
=L⁡(d~i,πi)+η​𝔼i​[1H​∑t=0H−1et]\displaystyle=L(\tilde{d}_{i},\pi_{i})+\eta\,\mathbb{E}_{i}\Big[\tfrac{1}{H}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}e_{t}\Big]
=L⁡(d~i,πi)+η​e¯i\displaystyle=L(\tilde{d}_{i},\pi_{i})+\eta\,\bar{e}_{i}

∎

J.2.5 How much edited text a rollout carries

Lemma 5 (Edit budget).

Let yy be the learner’s rollout in round ii and y~\tilde{y} its correction, each of HH decisions by Definition 2, and let m=e⁡(y,y~)m=e(y,\tilde{y}) be the edit size, with ete_{t} as in Lemma 4. Then et≤me_{t}\leq m at every decision 0≤t<H0\leq t<H, and consequently

∑t=0H−1et≤m​H.\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}e_{t}\;\leq\;m\,H.
Proof.

Let uu index the tokens of yy and vv those of y~\tilde{y}. A monotone matching between them is a set Φ\Phi of pairs (u,v)(u,v) with yu=y~vy_{u}=\tilde{y}_{v}, whose order agrees on both sides: u<u′⇔v<v′u<u^{\prime}\iff v<v^{\prime} for distinct (u,v),(u′,v′)∈Φ(u,v),(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})\in\Phi. The matched tokens read in order form a common subsequence of yy and y~\tilde{y}, so a largest matching has |Φ|=|LCS⁡(y,y~)||\Phi|=|\mathrm{LCS}(y,\tilde{y})|. Take such a Φ\Phi. Since yy and y~\tilde{y} each have HH tokens, m=2​H−2​|Φ|m=2H-2|\Phi| by Definition 4. For a decision tt put Φt={(u,v)∈Φ:u≤t,v≤t}\Phi_{t}=\{(u,v)\in\Phi:u\leq t,\ v\leq t\}, the pairs falling inside both prefixes, whose matched tokens form a common subsequence of y1:ty_{1:t} and y~1:t\tilde{y}_{1:t}. Both coordinates increase along Φ\Phi, so max⁡(u,v)\max(u,v) does too, strictly; every pair outside Φt\Phi_{t} has max⁡(u,v)≥t+1\max(u,v)\geq t+1, and distinct pairs take distinct values there, so

|Φ∖Φt|≤H−t.\big|\Phi\setminus\Phi_{t}\big|\;\leq\;H-t. (8)

Therefore

et\displaystyle e_{t} =2t−2|LCS(y1:t,y~1:t)|\displaystyle=2t-2\,\big|\mathrm{LCS}(y_{1:t},\tilde{y}_{1:t})\big| (by Definition 4)
≤2​t−2​|Φt|\displaystyle\leq 2t-2\,|\Phi_{t}| (Φt\Phi_{t} is a matching)
=2​t−2​|Φ|+2​|Φ∖Φt|\displaystyle=2t-2\,|\Phi|+2\,\big|\Phi\setminus\Phi_{t}\big|
≤2​t−2​|Φ|+2​(H−t)\displaystyle\leq 2t-2\,|\Phi|+2\,(H-t) (by (8))
=2​H−2​|Φ|=m\displaystyle=2H-2\,|\Phi|\;=\;m (by Definition 4)

Summing over the HH decisions gives the claim. ∎

An insertion early in the answer shifts every later prefix, and a count of mismatched positions would read that shift as a rewrite of the whole suffix. Definition 4 charges it at the size of the insertion instead, which is why the drift of Theorem 1 scales with mm and not with HH.

J.2.6 The bound

Theorem 1 of Sec. 5 states that under Definitions 2 and 3, Assumption 1, an idealized projector and mm the mean edit size over the rounds,

mini≤M⁡[J⋆−J⁡(πi)]≤H​Δmax​(ε~+γ~M)⏟fit and optimization+η​m​H⏟corrected-prefix drift.\min_{i\leq M}\big[J^{\star}-J(\pi_{i})\big]\;\leq\;\underbrace{H\,\Delta_{\max}\,\big(\tilde{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}_{M}\big)}_{\text{fit and optimization}}\;+\;\underbrace{\eta\,m\,H}_{\text{corrected-prefix drift}}.
Proof of Theorem 1.
mini≤M⁡[J⋆−J⁡(πi)]\displaystyle\min_{i\leq M}[J^{\star}-J(\pi_{i})] ≤1M​∑i=1M[J⋆−J⁡(πi)]\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}[J^{\star}-J(\pi_{i})]
≤HM​∑iL⁡(dπi,πi)\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{H}{M}\sum_{i}L(d^{\pi_{i}},\pi_{i}) (by Lemma 2)
≤HM​∑iL⁡(d~i,πi)+η​H​e¯\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{H}{M}\sum_{i}L(\tilde{d}_{i},\pi_{i})+\eta H\bar{e} (by Lemma 4)
≤HΔmax⋅1M∑iε~i(πi)+ηHe¯\displaystyle\leq H\Delta_{\max}\cdot\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{i})+\eta H\bar{e} (by Lemma 3)
≤H​Δmax​(ε~+γ~M)+η​H​e¯\displaystyle\leq H\Delta_{\max}(\tilde{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}_{M})+\eta H\bar{e} (by Definition 5)
≤H​Δmax​(ε~+γ~M)+η​m​H\displaystyle\leq H\Delta_{\max}(\tilde{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}_{M})+\eta\,m\,H (by Lemma 5)

where e¯=1M​∑ie¯i\bar{e}=\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i}\bar{e}_{i}. Lemma 5 bounds round ii by its own edit size, H​e¯i=𝔼i​[∑t=0H−1et]≤mi​HH\bar{e}_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{i}\big[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}e_{t}\big]\leq m_{i}\,H, so e¯≤1M​∑imi=m\bar{e}\leq\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i}m_{i}=m; no bound on the largest round is needed. ∎

J.2.7 Rate in the number of rounds

Proposition 1 (Convex reference rate).

Let Π\Pi and Θ\Theta be as in Sec. J.1, and suppose in addition that θ↦ε~i​(πθ)\theta\mapsto\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{\theta}) is convex on Θ\Theta for every ii, with gradient bound G=max⁡supθ∈Θi⁡∥∇θε~i​(πθ)∥G=\max_{i}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lVert\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{\theta})\rVert. Then projected online gradient descent on Θ\Theta with step size α=D/(G​M)\alpha=D/(G\sqrt{M}) attains γ~M≤D​G/M\tilde{\gamma}_{M}\leq DG/\sqrt{M}.

Proof.

Since Π\Pi is parameterized by Θ\Theta, the minimum over π∈Π\pi\in\Pi in Definition 5 is a minimum over θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. Write θ⋆∈arg⁡min⁡∑iθ∈Θ⁡ε~i​(πθ)\theta^{\star}\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\sum_{i}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{\theta}) for a minimiser, so that the comparator in the definition and the comparator in the analysis are the same point. Then, with gi=∇θε~i​(πθi)g_{i}=\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{\theta_{i}}),

M​γ~M\displaystyle M\tilde{\gamma}_{M} =∑iε~i​(πθi)−∑iε~i​(πθ⋆)\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{\theta_{i}})-\sum_{i}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi_{\theta^{\star}}) (by Definition 5)
≤∑igi⊤​(θi−θ⋆)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i}g_{i}^{\top}(\theta_{i}-\theta^{\star}) (convexity)
≤D22​α+α2​M​G2\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{D^{2}}{2\alpha}+\tfrac{\alpha}{2}MG^{2} (potential 12​α​∥θi−θ⋆∥2\tfrac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert\theta_{i}-\theta^{\star}\rVert^{2} telescopes)
≤D​G​M\displaystyle\leq DG\sqrt{M} (at α=D/(G​M)\alpha=D/(G\sqrt{M}))

where DD is the Euclidean diameter of Θ\Theta and GG the gradient bound. Dividing by MM gives γ~M≤D​G/M\tilde{\gamma}_{M}\leq DG/\sqrt{M}. ∎

Remark 1 (Scope of the rate).

Proposition 1 is the standard online-convex-optimization guarantee, stated to show how regret decays in the number of rounds. Its convexity hypothesis does not hold for a neural policy. Theorem 1 uses only γ~M\tilde{\gamma}_{M} as defined, so nothing below depends on Proposition 1; the O⁡(1/M)O(1/\sqrt{M}) form should be read as a convex reference point.

J.2.8 Reading the bound

Corollary 1 (Edit size affects the horizon dependence).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, the drift term has two extremes:

  1. (a)

    minimal edits, m=O⁡(1)m=O(1), give drift O⁡(η​H)O(\eta H);

  2. (b)

    a correction rewriting the whole answer, m=Θ⁡(H)m=\Theta(H), gives drift O⁡(η​H2)O(\eta H^{2}).

The quantity being bounded is itself of order HH, since the return lies in [0,H][0,H] by Definition 2. Read against that scale, case (a) puts the drift at the same order as the fit term and the bound is informative, while case (b) puts it an order above the trivial bound J⋆−J≤HJ^{\star}-J\leq H and the bound says nothing. The horizon dependence is therefore linear at one end and quadratic at the other, and what selects between them is the edit we choose rather than any property of the environment.

J.2.9 Scope of the analysis

Remark 2 (The analysis assumes a dense per-token reward).

Definition 2 makes the reward token-additive with rtok∈[0,1]r_{\mathrm{tok}}\in[0,1], so a rollout’s return is at most HH and the trivial bound on J⋆−J⁡(π)J^{\star}-J(\pi) is HH. The experiments verify only the final answer, a single 00–11 outcome, under which the trivial bound is 11. The drift term η​m​H\eta mH is therefore informative only where η​m\eta m is small: the guarantee is a statement about the dense-reward model, and the per-token credit it assumes is not what the verifier supplies.

Remark 3 (A statement about horizon dependence, not about algorithm identity).

Setting et≡0e_{t}\equiv 0, which corresponds to a projector queried at every mistake on the learner’s own prefix so that no edited token enters a conditioning prefix, removes the drift and leaves H​Δmax​(ε~+γ~M)H\Delta_{\max}(\tilde{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}_{M}), the shape of the DAgger guarantee (Ross et al., 2011). The linear–quadratic dichotomy of Corollary 1 is the same dichotomy that separates DAgger from behavior cloning. It does not follow that projected distillation is either algorithm: minimal-edit projection does not query a projector at every visited state and carries a drift term DAgger does not have, and a full rewrite is not behavior cloning for the reason in Remark 4. The correspondence is between rates.

Remark 4 (The drift does not vanish under a perfect fit).

In Ross et al. (2011) the quadratic term for behavior cloning scales with the fit error, so a learner that imitates perfectly suffers no compounding. The drift η​m​H\eta mH of Theorem 1 carries no factor of ε~\tilde{\varepsilon}. A learner that matches the projector exactly at every corrected prefix still pays it, because the mismatch between d~i\tilde{d}_{i} and dπid^{\pi_{i}} is exogenous, fixed by the edit that was chosen, rather than a consequence of imperfect fitting.

Remark 5 (The analyzed loss is not the deployed loss).

Theorem 1 is proved for the 00–11 disagreement of Definition 5. Three consequences.

First, no gradient method minimizes a 00–11 loss. Following Ross et al. (2011) we state the guarantee for the 00–11 loss and note that any convex upper bound may be substituted, with ε~\tilde{\varepsilon} and γ~M\tilde{\gamma}_{M} read as the floor and regret of that surrogate; the bound holds verbatim with a larger ε~\tilde{\varepsilon}.

Second, cross-entropy on the correction is such a bound. Since log⁡p≤p−1\log p\leq p-1 for p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], we have 1−π⁡(w⋆∣s~)≤−log⁡π⁡(w⋆∣s~)1-\pi(w^{\star}\mid\tilde{s})\leq-\log\pi(w^{\star}\mid\tilde{s}), so Theorem 1 covers maximum-likelihood fine-tuning on the projection.

Third, the deployed objective is not covered. The recipe minimizes a diff-localized contrast on the changed spans together with a self-SFT term on the learner’s own correct rollouts. A preference contrast is not an upper bound on the disagreement with the projector: it can be reduced by lowering the likelihood of y−y^{-} without raising that of y+y^{+}, so a small contrast loss does not imply a small ε~\tilde{\varepsilon}. The analysis characterizes the target: how far the correction lies from the attempt, the quantity the edit-size experiment varies and the one both objectives share. It does not characterize the contrast.

Corollary 2 (A projector that is not optimal).

Suppose the projector’s token forfeits δ⁡(s~)≔Δ⁡(s~,w⋆​(s~))≥0\delta(\tilde{s})\coloneqq\Delta(\tilde{s},w^{\star}(\tilde{s}))\geq 0 rather than nothing, and let δ¯\bar{\delta} be its average over the corrected prefixes. Then, under the remaining hypotheses of Theorem 1,

mini≤M⁡[J⋆−J⁡(πi)]≤H​δ¯+H​Δmax​(ε~+γ~M)+η​m​H.\min_{i\leq M}\big[J^{\star}-J(\pi_{i})\big]\;\leq\;H\bar{\delta}\;+\;H\,\Delta_{\max}\,(\tilde{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}_{M})\;+\;\eta\,m\,H.
Proof.

The term π⁡(w⋆∣s~)​Δ​(s~,w⋆)\pi(w^{\star}\mid\tilde{s})\,\Delta(\tilde{s},w^{\star}) dropped in Lemma 3 no longer vanishes, so that lemma reads L⁡(d~i,π)≤δ¯+Δmax​ε~i​(π)L(\tilde{d}_{i},\pi)\leq\bar{\delta}+\Delta_{\max}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}(\pi). Substituting it at the Lemma 3 step of Theorem 1 adds H​δ¯H\bar{\delta}, every term there already carrying the factor HH from Lemma 2, and leaves the rest of the chain unchanged. ∎

The two error sources stay separate: δ¯\bar{\delta} measures the projector and shrinks only with a better one, while ε~\tilde{\varepsilon} measures the policy class and shrinks with a larger one.
